title: About
text:
Muscle powers every movement an animal makes — from the molecular motors inside a single fiber to the coordinated mechanics of running, balancing, and recovering from a stumble. The Integrative Movement Sciences Institute (IMSI) brings together researchers from across the United States to study how that works, and we are excited that you are interested in joining us through this curriculum!
IMSI is a National Science Foundation Biology Integration Institute, headquartered at the University of California, Irvine. Our network spans more than 20 institutions and cuts across biomechanics, muscle physiology, biophysics, sensorimotor neuroscience, and rehabilitation science — fields that rarely talk to each other, but that together tell a fuller story of how movement happens.
The modules here are taught by the researchers doing this work. They cover a range of topics and levels — from introductory overviews to advanced experimental and computational methods — and are designed to be explored freely or followed as part of a curated learning pathway. The curriculum is free, fully online, and always growing.
To learn more about IMSI’s research, people, and programs visit MovementScience.uci.edu.

title: Series elasticity
text:
Workshop


Presented by: Dr. Manny Azizi


What is in-series elasticity?
In-series elastic elements are compliant structures positioned in series with muscle that store mechanical energy during loading and return it during recoil; they appear throughout the animal kingdom, from resilin-based structures in invertebrates to the tendons and aponeuroses of vertebrates. Vertebrate tendons are composed of collagen organized hierarchically from tropocollagen molecules into fibrils, fibers, and fascicles. Tendons are metabolically quiet tissues with slow collagen turnover, meaning that tendon remodeling lags substantially behind muscle remodeling during periods of rapid change such as strength training or injury recovery.



Tendon material properties: from nonlinearity to viscoelasticity
Plotting force against deformation in a stretched tendon reveals a nonlinear curve: a compliant toe region, arising from the progressive straightening of crimped collagen fibers at low strains, gives way to a roughly linear region whose slope—normalized for cross-sectional area and gauge length—yields the elastic modulus. Tendons are viscoelastic rather than purely elastic: repeated loading-unloading cycles enclose a hysteresis loop indicating energy loss, and the material also exhibits stress relaxation under constant deformation. Key locomotor tendons are highly resilient, returning approximately 90–93% of stored energy per cycle (Ker, Dimery, and Alexander, Journal of Zoology, 1986). These viscoelastic properties mean that effective tendon stiffness is loading-rate dependent and cannot be fully captured by a simple spring model.



A framework for tendon function: three modes of operation
Tendon function can be organized into three operational modes that parallel the motor-strut-brake framework used to describe muscle function: power conservation, in which cyclic elastic storage and return reduces the metabolic cost of steady locomotion; power amplification, in which tendon loading and rapid recoil during explosive movements boosts instantaneous mechanical power beyond what muscle alone can deliver; and power attenuation, in which the tendon acts as a mechanical buffer during high-power impact loading. Each mode is determined by the mechanical context in which the muscle-tendon unit operates.



Power conservation during cyclic locomotion
During cyclic locomotion such as running and hopping, tendons allow muscles to generate force nearly isometrically while the tendon absorbs and returns mechanical energy across each stride, minimizing the mechanical work performed by the fibers. This mechanism is demonstrated clearly in kangaroos and tammar wallabies, where metabolic cost becomes largely independent of hopping speed once the animals transition to a hopping gait—because the gastrocnemius and plantaris muscles operate near-isometrically while the tendon cycles energy at the ankle joint (Dawson & Taylor, Nature, 1973; Biewener, Konieczynski, & Baudinette, J Exp Biol, 1998). The metabolic advantage of near-isometric operation reflects the cost-of-force hypothesis: when a muscle shortens during contraction, force capacity falls along the force-velocity relationship, requiring additional muscle volume to be recruited to maintain support forces, and it is the volume of muscle under load that drives metabolic cost (Holt, Roberts, & Askew, J Exp Biol, 2014). Tendons that prevent fascicle shortening therefore reduce total active muscle volume, not mechanical work output directly.



Power amplification: latch-mediated spring actuation
Explosive movements require peak mechanical power that can exceed what muscle alone can deliver, because the force-velocity trade-off limits the power available from direct muscle contraction. In latch-mediated spring actuation, the muscle (motor) slowly loads energy into the tendon (spring) while a latch—implemented in vertebrate limbs by joint geometry that provides low mechanical advantage at extreme flexion—prevents premature movement; rapid latch release then delivers stored energy at higher peak power than the muscle could sustain directly (Ilton et al., Science, 2018). For a given muscle, an optimal tendon stiffness maximizes stored energy: a spring that is too compliant allows excessive muscle shortening and force-capacity loss, while one that is too stiff allows too little deformation to store meaningful energy. In frog jumping, muscle shortening and tendon recoil contribute concurrently during takeoff, which explains why performance is temperature-sensitive even though purely elastic recoil is not—the temperature-dependent component is ongoing muscle power output during the unloading phase.



Scaling: when do springs help?
The advantage of spring-driven actuation is strongly body-size dependent: for very small animals, elastic storage and rapid recoil dramatically outperforms direct muscle actuation across multiple performance metrics, while for larger animals the increasing inertia of the load progressively erodes this power advantage (Ilton et al., Science, 2018). Above a size-dependent crossover, the benefit of spring actuation diminishes substantially, and animals near this transition may exploit both elastic storage and direct muscle power simultaneously. Whether a given animal benefits more from spring actuation or direct muscle contraction depends on body mass, muscle mechanical properties, and the specific performance metric being considered.



Power attenuation: the tendon as a mechanical buffer
During impact loading, in-series tendons protect muscle fibers through two complementary mechanisms: the activated muscle can shorten against the incoming force even as the whole muscle-tendon unit lengthens—because the tendon absorbs the external deformation—moving fibers to shorter, safer positions on the force-length curve before any fascicle stretch occurs; subsequently, the tendon reloads the fibers at a lower velocity than the original impact, attenuating the mechanical power delivered to the sarcomeres (Konow, Azizi, & Roberts, Proc R Soc B, 2012). Anticipatory muscle activation before impact promotes greater initial fascicle shortening and a more protective shift in operating length, as demonstrated in experiments where varying activation onset by tens of milliseconds altered fascicle operating length during the ensuing stretch. Faster deactivation kinetics allow the tendon to recoil more rapidly, imposing higher stretch velocities on the fibers—a proposed mechanism for the greater susceptibility of fast-twitch fibers to eccentric damage, though this remains a hypothesis requiring direct experimental test. An underappreciated consequence of in-series compliance is that muscle spindle (Ia) afferents may receive signals that do not accurately reflect external mechanics when fascicles shorten while the joint flexes, making anticipatory feed-forward motor commands essential for appropriate pre-contact muscle conditioning in highly compliant tendon systems.

title: Scaling and dimensional analysis
section: Energy fluctuation patterns of walking and running in terrestrial gaits
text:
Energy fluctuation patterns of walking and running in terrestrial gaits
Walking and running gaits exhibit fundamentally different energy fluctuation patterns that can be understood through spring-loaded inverted pendulum models. In walking, the body operates as an inverted pendulum vaulting over a relatively stiff limb, with the leg acting at nearly fixed length during stance (as humans typically lock out the knee). This creates an out-of-phase relationship between gravitational potential energy and kinetic energy: when the foot first contacts the ground, velocity is at maximum, then kinetic energy converts to potential energy as the body reaches peak height at mid-stance, before reaccelerating and converting potential energy back to kinetic energy in the second half of stance. This passive energy exchange between kinetic and potential energies makes walking economical, requiring minimal external mechanical work on the center of mass. In contrast, running is characterized by bouncing motion where the leg acts as a compliant spring. The center of mass height decreases during stance rather than increasing, resulting in both kinetic energy and potential energy decreasing during the first half of stance and increasing during the second half. These in-phase fluctuations of external mechanical energies mean there cannot be an exchange between kinetic and potential energy; instead, energy is stored in elastic springs within the connective tissues (tendons, ligaments, and muscles) during the first half of stance and released during the second half. The spring-loaded inverted pendulum model, which combines both inverted pendulum and mass-spring dynamics, can account for the coupling between these two modes of motion and successfully predict ground reaction force patterns across diverse bipedal species.

title: Scaling and dimensional analysis
section: Principles of scaling with geometric similarity
text:
Principles of scaling with geometric similarity
The principle of isometric scaling (or geometric similarity) reveals fundamental challenges that arise when animals increase in body size while maintaining the same shape. When an object doubles in linear dimensions while preserving shape, its cross-sectional areas increase by the square of the length change (length²), while volume and mass increase by the cube of the length change (length³). This differential scaling creates a critical biomechanical problem: the ratio of cross-sectional area to mass decreases with increasing size (specifically, as one over length). Since strength in musculoskeletal tissues is proportional to cross-sectional area (scaling as length²) while loading is proportional to body mass (scaling as length³), animals that simply scale up geometrically become relatively weaker as they grow larger. This means larger animals experience relatively higher stresses on their tissues unless they compensate through shape changes. One observed compensation is that large animals adopt more upright, straight-legged postures, which align the bones vertically to better support body weight and reduce the muscular effort required to stand upright. This fundamental scaling challenge—that weight scales much faster than strength—has profound implications for how animals of different sizes must be structured and how they move, leading to systematic changes in both anatomy and locomotor function across the size range from the smallest shrews to the largest elephants.

title: Scaling and dimensional analysis
text:
Dynamic similarity hypothesis
The dynamic similarity hypothesis, developed by Alexander and colleagues in the 1970s-80s, proposes that if locomotor function remains constant across animals of different sizes, then size-related differences should disappear once data are normalized to dimensionless values using a standard set of characteristic physical quantities. For legged terrestrial locomotion, the appropriate base quantities are body mass, leg length, and gravity, derived from considering both inverted pendulum dynamics (with characteristic period related to √(L/g)) and mass-spring dynamics (with characteristic frequency related to √(k/m)). According to this hypothesis, all lengths and distances should be normalized by leg length, forces by body weight (mg), time by the characteristic pendular period √(L/g), frequency by √(g/L), and velocity by √(gL). An important dimensionless quantity is Froude number (v²/gL), which represents the ratio of inertial forces to gravitational forces and equals the square of dimensionless velocity; it is physically impossible for legged systems to walk at Froude numbers greater than one because centripetal accelerations would exceed gravitational acceleration. When locomotion data from species spanning vastly different body sizes are normalized using these dimensionless quantities, the dynamic similarity hypothesis predicts that all variation should collapse onto a single relationship. However, as demonstrated in the bird locomotion data, perfect collapse does not occur—while normalization does reduce variation significantly (particularly in stride frequency), systematic differences remain, with larger birds using relatively higher stride frequencies and shorter stride lengths than smaller birds. These deviations from perfect dynamic similarity reveal functionally important differences in how animals of different sizes actually move, such as large birds employing more vertically bouncy gaits while small birds use flatter center of mass trajectories, reflecting different mechanical strategies and constraints across the body size spectrum.

title: Biophysical muscle models
text:
Overview

Why Model Muscles?
When we move, “everything comes from the muscle” — muscles pull our bones and drive our bodies through space. To simulate, study, or predict movement and posture control, researchers need accurate models of how much force a muscle generates given its activation, length, and velocity. Muscle models are used in two main ways: (1) forward simulation of movement, such as modeling a balance response to a perturbation on a moving platform; and (2) inverse estimation of muscle forces from motion capture and EMG measurements, for example using tools like OpenSim.


The Conventional Approach: Hill-Type Models
The Hill-type muscle model is the most widely used approach in biomechanics. In this phenomenological model, muscle force is estimated as the product of three quantities: activation, a force-length curve, and a force-velocity curve. These curves capture the known fact that muscles produce maximum isometric force at an optimal length and that force decreases at higher shortening velocities. However, the Hill-type model does not capture any history-dependent properties — muscle force is simply a function of current activation, length, and velocity, with no way to account for what the muscle was doing beforehand.


History Dependence: A Problem for Hill-Type Models
Real muscles exhibit substantial history dependence across multiple levels. At the fiber level, a single muscle fiber subjected to a conditioning stretch produces different forces during two portions of lengthening that involve the same velocity and length change — because one portion follows a resting state and the other follows prior movement. At the muscle level, data show different force outputs for the same length trajectory depending on what history preceded it. At the movement level, the “knee pendulum test” demonstrates that a leg dropped from the same height oscillates differently depending on whether it was held still or moving beforehand. In each case, the Hill-type model would predict the same force for identical current states, even though actual forces differ.


The Biophysical Approach: Cross-Bridge Models
The biophysical muscle model is built on the molecular mechanism of active force generation. Active force in muscle comes from cross-bridges — molecular bindings between myosin (thick filament) and actin (thin filament) deep inside muscle fibers; passive force comes from other structural elements. In the simplest version of the model, a cross-bridge is treated as a spring that can exist in two states: attached or detached. Within a muscle, many cross-bridges exist at different displacement lengths from their resting state. The model tracks the distribution of bound cross-bridges across those lengths at each time step, computing how many will transition between states using attachment and detachment rate functions. Attachment rate is highest near zero displacement (resting length) and decreases as cross-bridges are pulled further from equilibrium; detachment rate increases with displacement. Total active muscle force is then the sum of spring forces from all bound cross-bridges.


History Dependence as an Emergent Property
A key insight from the cross-bridge framework is that history dependence arises naturally — it is “an emerging property, rather than we explicitly kept track of the history of everything.” At any instant, the distribution of bound cross-bridges reflects the accumulated history of muscle activation and movement. If a muscle arrives at the same length and activation level via two different paths, it carries different cross-bridge distributions and therefore generates different forces — exactly the behavior observed experimentally, and exactly what the Hill-type model cannot reproduce.


Extending the Model: More States and Calcium Activation
The basic two-state (attached/detached) model can be extended by adding additional states. For example, myosin can enter a “super-relaxed” state in which it is not ready to bind to actin. More importantly, the availability of actin binding sites is controlled by calcium: when the nervous system activates a muscle, calcium ions are released into the muscle fiber, enabling actin sites to become available for cross-bridge binding. Calcium concentration is therefore the activation control signal in simulations. Whether to use a two-state, three-state, or higher-order model depends on which phenomena the researcher needs to reproduce.


Comparing Models: When Does the Transient Matter?
An interactive MATLAB GUI — originally developed for a tutorial at the International Society for Biomechanics (ISB) annual meeting — allows direct comparison of cross-bridge model predictions to Hill-type model predictions. Overall, the two approaches produce comparable force estimates at steady state. The critical difference lies in transient behavior, particularly at the onset of lengthening or shortening. For questions about overall force at steady state, the Hill-type model may be sufficient; for questions where transient force development matters, the cross-bridge model may be more appropriate.


Application: Balance Control and Short-Range Stiffness
Dr. Ryu applies the cross-bridge model to study how humans recover balance after postural perturbations. Experimentally, different joints show distinct torque patterns: the hip develops torque rapidly and then decreases, while ankle torque rises more slowly and remains elevated. When a conventional Hill-type model is used to simulate the first 100 milliseconds after a perturbation, it overestimates the initial body movement — an issue that prior work has linked to the absence of short-range stiffness in the model. Dr. Ryu’s approach grounds this stiffness in cross-bridge mechanics, with the hope that stiffness arising from the physiological process will prove more generalizable across perturbation directions and amplitudes than stiffness prescribed by hand. Coupling the cross-bridge model to an inverted pendulum with tendons of varying compliance suggests that joint-specific torque patterns may reflect a gradient in tendon compliance across the lower limb — a hypothesis that preliminary literature values appear to support. The resulting simulation captures most of the key trends seen in human perturbation data across joints.

title: Balance, stability, and agility
text:
Overview

Evaluating Balance Metrics: A Systematic Comparison
A paper from Steve Collins’ lab at Stanford used a rigorous experimental design to test how well six commonly used balance metrics actually detect imbalance. The study applied two types of challenges simultaneously: large-scale perturbations using a multi-directional cable system called the “Bump’em” (attached to participants’ trunks during treadmill walking), and steady disruptions to the physiological systems that normally support balance — blocking vision, locking the ankles, and using pneumatic air jets fired at the swing leg to disturb foot placement. Ten subjects completed the protocol. The six metrics tested were: step width, step time, step placement predictability, Lyapunov exponent, margin of stability, and center-of-mass displacement. Performance varied substantially across metrics. Foot placement predictability outperformed all other measures globally, while center-of-mass displacement alone performed no better than chance at detecting whether a person was in an unbalanced state.


Step Placement Predictability
The step placement predictability framework is built on the observation that at mid-stance, a person’s center-of-mass position and velocity can be used in a simple linear map to predict where the next footfall will land. This strong linear relationship between mid-stance center-of-mass state and subsequent foot placement suggests that a complex, nonlinear locomotion system may use a relatively simple control rule to regulate balance. The fact that this metric also came out on top in the Collins lab’s systematic comparison provides two lines of evidence supporting it as a useful measure of balance control.


Angular Momentum as a Balance Measure
Whole-body angular momentum is another important balance measure. From a physics standpoint, keeping angular momentum near zero on average prevents a person from pitching forward to the ground; angular momentum represents the combined rotational contributions of all body segments. Ground reaction forces produce moments around the body’s center of mass that continually regulate this quantity. Work by Anne Silverman showed that even during steady walking (without perturbations), populations at higher fall risk differ measurably in how they regulate angular momentum. For example, amputees show larger-amplitude swings in frontal-plane angular momentum compared to non-amputees, with the difference most pronounced at slow walking speeds. This suggests that frontal-plane angular momentum fluctuation during steady gait may serve as a useful marker of balance impairment. Studying angular momentum only during steady walking is limited, however; understanding balance fully requires also examining how angular momentum responds to large-scale perturbations.


Perturbation Experiments and Exoskeleton Assistance
Several perturbation paradigms can be used to study balance beyond steady-state walking. One uses the “Karen” system — a treadmill mounted on a Stewart platform — to deliver phase-locked surface perturbations during walking across 96 combinations of magnitude, direction, and gait phase. Whole-body angular momentum is tracked before, during, and after each perturbation to assess how well the person’s system returns to its steady pattern; the recovery process typically spans multiple steps. Another paradigm uses treadmill belt slips timed to either early or late stance, which either inject or remove mechanical energy from the leg. After a belt slip, the contralateral knee’s next step appears to be the primary joint compensating for the energy change. A passive hip spring exoskeleton tested in this paradigm did not significantly reduce deviations in angular momentum or mechanical energy following the perturbation, possibly because a passive spring cannot modulate mechanical work with optimal timing.
In a standing balance exoskeleton study conducted in collaboration with Dr. Lena Ting, an ankle exoskeleton was programmed to apply plantar flexion torque faster than the human nervous system’s own response latency in reaction to a backward surface perturbation. Balance was measured using a psychometric curve approach: perturbation size was progressively increased until participants took a protective step, identifying the size at which stepping occurred more than 50% of the time. Only the condition in which the exoskeleton acted faster than the human’s own response improved this threshold. EMG and ultrasound data further showed that in the fast exoskeleton condition, calf muscle stretch was reduced — yet balance still improved. This suggests that the improvement did not rely on enhanced local ankle reflexes but on a global center-of-mass-level strategy in which information from across the body is integrated to coordinate the balance response.


Defining Stability and Agility Through Energy and Limit Cycles
A conceptual framework for defining and measuring both stability and agility uses a simple model of rhythmic movement. The experimental platform is a motorized ankle dynamometer: participants lie prone on a table, and their plantar flexors perform a cyclical task that feels like vertical bouncing against a gravitational load, even though only the ankle joint is involved. Participants follow a metronome and aim to maintain a target peak ankle angle. The resulting movement can be represented as a limit cycle in a phase portrait (joint angle vs. angular velocity), and the total mechanical energy of the system (kinetic plus gravitational potential) can be calculated at any point on that cycle.
Stability is then defined as the time constant for the system’s energy to return to its nominal limit-cycle energy (E₀) after the motor injects a perturbation. A shorter time constant indicates a more stable system. Agility is defined using the same energy framework but in a different direction: instead of being knocked off the limit cycle by a perturbation, the participant is given a new target (a higher or lower energy level), and agility is quantified by how quickly the system reaches the new target. A shorter transition time, or equivalently a higher average power over the transition, indicates greater agility. This approach uses a common energy currency, making it possible to compare the costs and timescales of stabilization, agile transitions, and metabolic efficiency within one framework.

title: The brain and balance
text:
Overview

Why Balance Control Matters
Balance control is foundational to all voluntary movement: infants must achieve stable standing before locomotion is possible, and loss of balance leads to falls that are a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in adults over 65. Because balance depends on the coordinated function of sensory, motor, and cognitive systems, it is impaired across a remarkably broad range of conditions — from musculoskeletal injury to neurological and psychiatric disorders. This breadth makes balance a tractable model system for studying fundamental principles of motor control, and mechanisms underlying corrective standing responses generalize to corrective torques during perturbed walking as well.


Balance as an Automatic Behavior
Under ordinary conditions, balance is governed automatically by subcortical circuits — the spinal cord and brainstem — without requiring conscious attention, much as breathing requires no deliberate effort. As task difficulty increases or as aging and neurological disease progress, control shifts toward higher cortical circuits, where processing is more deliberate but draws on more limited cognitive resources. This shift explains the clinical observation that individuals with fall risk slow down when asked to walk and perform a cognitive task simultaneously: balance has begun to compete for the same pool of cortical resources as the secondary task.


The Sensory Foundations of Balance
Maintaining balance requires answering three questions simultaneously: which way is up (postural orientation), whether the body is falling (equilibrium), and the current configuration of body segments (posture). No single sensory system answers all three: vision provides environmental context but cannot distinguish self-motion from world motion; the vestibular system detects head acceleration and gravity but conflates tilt with lateral acceleration; cutaneous receptors in the foot sole map ground reaction force distribution; and muscle spindle proprioceptors encode body segment configuration. The nervous system continuously integrates and reweights these signals based on their reliability in the current context — a process that can fail when one modality is compromised or when sensory channels conflict.


Perceptual Thresholds and Whole-Body Motion Perception
Effective balance correction requires first perceiving which direction the body is falling; the nervous system must identify perturbation direction before selecting the appropriate muscular response. Perceptual thresholds for whole-body motion direction can be measured psychophysically: participants receive paired platform perturbations at varying angular offsets and judge whether the two directions felt the same or different, yielding a psychometric curve whose threshold (angular acuity) and slope (perceptual sensitivity) are estimated separately. Average thresholds of approximately 9.5 degrees have been measured in young adults; thresholds are elevated in older adults, further elevated in Parkinson’s disease, and in some stroke patients have been observed approaching 50 degrees — a deficit magnitude that may contribute more to impaired balance than muscle weakness alone.


Neural Hierarchies: Spinal Cord, Brainstem, and Cortex
Balance responses are organized across three hierarchical levels with distinct latencies and functional roles. Spinal cord circuits respond at approximately 50 ms and produce joint-level stretch reflexes and co-contraction that stiffen the body against small deviations, but cannot compute whole-body falling direction. Brainstem circuits respond at approximately 100 ms and integrate multi-sensory signals to select muscle strategies appropriate for the actual direction of whole-body motion — explaining why the calf muscle correctly shuts off and reverses when a forward platform tilt rotates the body backward, a computation impossible with spinal proprioceptive reflexes alone. Cortical responses arrive later and govern strategic decisions such as whether to step or grab for support; elevated cortical involvement, as seen in aging and Parkinson’s disease, is associated with greater co-contraction, impaired direction selectivity, and narrowed cognitive resources for concurrent tasks.


Brain Activity During Balance: Beta Oscillations and the N1 Potential
Two cortical signals measurable by scalp EEG reliably track individual differences in balance performance. Pre-perturbation beta oscillations (13–30 Hz) predict whole-body motion perception thresholds on a trial-by-trial basis — higher beta power in the moments before a perturbation predicts worse discrimination — and Parkinson’s disease is associated with pathologically elevated resting beta in sensorimotor circuits that correlates with clinical balance scores. The N1 potential — a negative deflection of approximately 50 microvolts over the supplementary motor area — is interpreted as a neural index of perturbation challenge: it is larger for surprising, severe, or feared perturbations; it attenuates with repetition and predictability in healthy adults; and this modulation is absent or reduced in Parkinson’s disease and stroke, where the response may remain equally large regardless of how many times the perturbation has been experienced.


Cognitive Set Shifting and Motor Inflexibility
Cognitive set shifting — the executive capacity to update behavioral strategy when task rules change — is reliably linked to fall risk in older adults and people with Parkinson’s disease, and is assessed clinically with the Trail Making Test (the additional time for Part B beyond Part A isolates the cognitive cost of rule-switching). This function has a direct motor counterpart: motor set shifting is the ability to update muscle coordination patterns when the postural context changes, demonstrated by research from Horak and colleagues showing that healthy individuals rapidly attenuate lower-limb balance responses when repositioned from standing to seated, whereas people with Parkinson’s disease continue to activate lower-limb muscles appropriate for standing even in the seated condition. In older adults without clinical deficits, slower Trail Making Test B correlates with greater muscle co-contraction during perturbations — a postural stiffening strategy — and with inappropriate tibialis anterior activation at cortical latencies following backward perturbations, suggesting an inability to reliably discriminate perturbation direction rather than a deliberate change in strategy.

title: Ultrasound imaging
text:
Overview

Why Measuring Muscle Fascicle Length and Velocity Matters
The force-generating capacity of a muscle depends on the instantaneous position on its force–length and force–velocity curves, both of which are determined by fascicle length and shortening velocity relative to the muscle’s optimum. Measuring these quantities during natural movement reveals how a muscle’s operating capacity changes from moment to moment, informing understanding of why particular movement strategies are adopted. Research combining dynamometry with ultrasound has shown, for example, that human soleus operates near the ascending portion of the force–length plateau during walking, and that the preferred walk-to-run transition speed corresponds to fascicle lengths and shortening velocities that favor force production.


How Ultrasound Works
An ultrasound transducer emits high-frequency acoustic waves and detects the echoes reflected from tissue interfaces; software converts the speed and strength of returning echoes into a two-dimensional image. The brightness of a structure in the image depends on its echogenicity: anechoic structures such as blood and fluid appear dark, while highly echogenic structures such as bone, tendon, and connective tissue appear bright white. Bone surfaces reflect so strongly that ultrasound cannot penetrate further, producing a bright line with an acoustic shadow beneath it; musculoskeletal imaging is performed in B-mode (brightness mode), while Doppler mode is reserved for blood-flow velocity measurements.


Identifying Tissue Structures in Ultrasound Images
Muscle is recognizable by characteristic striations produced by interspersed connective tissue and aponeuroses. Tendons are echogenic and circular in cross-section, tapering in diameter along their length, whereas nerves maintain a consistent diameter; the clinical mnemonic VAN (vein–artery–nerve) — in which a pulsing, anechoic vessel is found adjacent to a brighter circular structure — helps locate nerves in an image. A transverse probe orientation is generally best for differentiating between structures, while a longitudinal orientation is preferred for visualizing and tracking fascicles.


Ultrasound Probe Setup and Integration with Motion Capture
Standard handheld clinical probes cannot be secured to a limb during dynamic movement; flat-form-factor probes designed for musculoskeletal biomechanics research are strapped directly to the skin, often alongside a foam block of similar dimensions to prevent probe rotation, and secured with cohesive bandage. Synchronization with motion capture and force plates is achieved by connecting the ultrasound module to a shared analog signal box and issuing a common trigger signal to start and stop recording across all devices simultaneously. When using Echo Wave software, a dedicated sync plug-in must be enabled for the system to register external trigger signals correctly.


Fascicle Tracking Software: UltraTimTrack and UlTrack
UltraTimTrack (implemented in MATLAB) fuses two computer-vision methods — optical flow, which tracks pixel motion between frames and tolerates image noise but can accumulate drift, and line detection, which operates on each frame independently and is drift-resistant but noise-sensitive — with a tunable weighting parameter that balances the two; a built-in sensitivity analysis function allows users to assess how this parameter affects the resulting length trace. UlTrack (v5.3, also MATLAB-based) uses optical flow alone and is better suited to slow, controlled movements; it includes a keyframe-correction feature that allows the user to anchor fascicle length at defined points in the movement cycle to remove accumulated drift. Both tools allow user-defined regions of interest between the deep and superficial aponeuroses, and fascicle coordinates from the Simple Muscle Architecture plug-in for ImageJ can be imported into UlTrack to reduce subjectivity in fascicle selection.


Recommended Acquisition Settings and Limitations
A frame rate of approximately 150 Hz is a practical trade-off between temporal resolution and image quality, with most current systems reaching a maximum of approximately 210–220 frames per second; below approximately 100–120 Hz, automated tracking methods show markedly increased noise. Higher frame rates are obtained by reducing image depth, image width, and the number of ultrasonic beams per scan — settings that trade image quality for temporal resolution. A field of view of approximately 50 mm depth by 40 mm width is typical for lower-limb fascicle tracking applications.


Advantages, Limitations, and Practical Considerations
Relative to implanted sonomicrometry sensors, ultrasound is non-invasive, provides contextual information about surrounding tissue motion, and is portable and straightforward to synchronize with other data-acquisition systems. Its principal limitations are a maximum temporal resolution of approximately 200 Hz at best image quality and reliance on computer-vision tracking algorithms that can accumulate error during fast or highly perturbed movements. In field deployments, portable probes can be combined with markerless motion capture systems; wireless ultrasound transmission carries substantial bandwidth costs relative to wired systems, and universal timestamping provides a practical strategy for post-hoc synchronization when hardware triggering is unavailable.

title: Data visualization and statistical inference for biomechanics
text:
Overview

Research goals and sources of variability
Scientific studies fall broadly into four categories: descriptive, methods-development, relational (correlations and regressions), and experimental (cause-and-effect). Understanding variability is central to research design: concomitant variation — change in a dependent variable when the independent variable is manipulated — enables causal inference; extraneous variability from inconsistent measurement or uncontrolled participant characteristics reduces the ability to detect true effects; and confounding variables can prevent causal conclusions altogether. Statistics provide tools for quantifying and attributing these sources of variability.


Anscombe’s Quartet: the limits of summary statistics
Anscombe’s Quartet consists of four datasets that are visually very different but share nearly identical descriptive statistics — means, standard deviations, regression slopes, intercepts, and R-squared values. This demonstrates that summary statistics alone cannot reveal the underlying structure of data: a linear model is appropriate for only one of the four datasets, while the others show curvature, outliers, or degenerate structure that makes the fitted line meaningless. The practical implication is to visualize data early and often throughout the analysis pipeline, from data collection through each subsequent processing step.


Making publication-ready figures in MATLAB
The choice of visualization method can either reveal or conceal the structure of data: a bar chart with error bars can make very different distributions appear similar in spread, while a dot plot showing individual data points and medians immediately reveals differences between them. Best practices for figure formatting include labeling all axes with full words and units, encoding all formatting choices in code using MATLAB’s set function so that figures can be regenerated automatically when analyses change, and specifying figure dimensions in centimeters to match intended print size. Figures should be saved in multiple formats — a MATLAB .fig file for later editing, a PDF for annotation, and a TIFF for journal submission — because TIFF preserves more image information than JPEG’s lossy compression.


Understanding p-values through simulation
A p-value is the probability of obtaining a result at least as extreme as the observed one if the null hypothesis were true. Simulating many independent studies in which the null hypothesis is known to be true by construction produces p-values distributed approximately uniformly between 0 and 1, with roughly 5% falling below 0.05 — giving concrete meaning to the false positive rate implied by the conventional significance threshold. A p-value does not indicate the scientific importance of a finding; with very large samples, p < 0.05 is achievable for effects too small to be practically meaningful.


Sample size, statistical power, and effect size
Statistical power, sample size, and effect size are interrelated: achieving a given power level to detect a specified effect size determines the required sample size, with higher desired power and smaller expected effect sizes both requiring larger samples. Conversely, researchers limited in the number of participants they can collect are best positioned to study effects likely to be large. An important distinction separates statistical significance from practical importance: effect sizes and their uncertainty are more informative than p-values alone, and determining what effect magnitude matters often requires domain-specific judgment, such as a minimally clinically important difference (for example, a 0.4 m/s change in walking speed) in applied settings.

title: Computational modeling
text:
Overview

Introduction to Computational Modeling in Muscle Biology
Computational modeling uses mathematics and computation to study complex biological systems across different organizational scales. In the context of muscle biology, models range from describing simple chemical reactions—such as how two molecular species combine to form a third, captured by a set of differential equations—all the way up to simulating the coordinated mechanics of many interacting filaments within a sarcomere. Dr. Tanner’s lab integrates computational modeling with biophysical experiments (primarily single-fiber mechanics using skinned fibers) to investigate the molecular mechanisms of muscle contraction. The proteins at the center of these models include the thin filaments (primarily actin), the thick filaments (myosin), and regulatory proteins such as troponin, tropomyosin, and myosin binding protein C.


A Brief History: The Hill Model
One of the earliest influential models of muscle force production was developed by A.V. Hill, who shared the 1922 Nobel Prize for linking heat production and mechanical work in muscles. The Hill model represented muscle as three components: a passive element, a contractile element, and a series element (which can be thought of as representing the tendon or other in-series compliance). Together these produced a force-length relationship with recognizable features: the passive component contributes little force at resting length but grows substantially at longer lengths; the active (contractile) component shows an ascending limb, a plateau, and a descending limb; and the total (combined) force reflects a trade-off between these two contributions. Despite its simplicity, this framework has remained widely useful for describing how muscle force changes with length.


Crossbridge Theory: The Huxley 1957 Model
A major conceptual advance came from Andrew Huxley’s 1957 paper, which introduced the idea that myosin crossbridges interact with actin binding sites in a position-dependent manner as the filaments slide past one another. In this model, the rate of crossbridge attachment (called f) and the rate of detachment (called g) both depend on the spatial position or distortion of the crossbridge—that is, how far the myosin head is displaced from its optimal alignment relative to the nearest actin binding site. When filaments are not moving (isometric conditions), a high proportion of crossbridges are bound and substantial force is generated. As shortening velocity increases, the distribution of bound crossbridges shifts and total force decreases, reproducing the well-known force-velocity relationship. A further refinement came from Huxley and Simmons in their 1971 paper, which proposed a crossbridge power stroke: a conformational change in the neck region of the myosin head (visible in structural data as the head moving from one angular position to another) that constitutes the force-generating event.


Spatially Explicit Two-Filament Models
Through much of the history of muscle modeling it was assumed that thick and thin filaments are rigid—that all the compliance in the system comes from the crossbridges themselves. If the filaments do not stretch, then the mechanical state of one actin–myosin pair is identical to every other pair, and a single interaction can represent the whole population. However, X-ray diffraction measurements from the mid-1990s provided evidence that both thick and thin filaments are themselves elastic (extensible). This finding meant that neighboring crossbridges along a filament can be in different mechanical states depending on whether and how their neighbors are bound, making a population-level spatial model necessary.
This motivated the two-filament spatially explicit model published by Daniel and colleagues in 1998. The model represented a half-sarcomere using 20 thick filament nodes (positions from which crossbridges extend) and 30 actin binding sites on the thin filament, with linear elastic springs connecting adjacent nodes along each filament. The different node counts reflect the different periodicities of the two filament types (approximately 43 nm for the thick filament and approximately 37 nm for the thin filament). Because solving large systems of ordinary or partial differential equations for position-dependent crossbridge kinetics is computationally difficult, the model used Monte Carlo (stochastic) algorithms in which crossbridge attachment and detachment are governed by probabilities derived from position-dependent rate functions rather than solved analytically.


Multiple Filament Models and Physiological Geometry
In the physiological sarcomere, the filament arrangement is not a simple one-to-one pairing: each thick filament interacts with six thin filaments, and each thin filament interacts with three thick filaments. Dr. Tanner’s doctoral work extended the two-filament framework to simulate this physiological lattice geometry. To avoid the edge effects that arise in a finite lattice, the model simulated 4 thick filaments and 8 thin filaments but applied periodic boundary conditions—effectively wrapping the edges of the simulated region onto each other to approximate an infinite lattice with a finite number of filaments. The model also incorporated calcium-dependent thin filament activation through a three-state kinetic cycle.
When compared to the two-filament model at the same calcium levels, the multiple-filament model predicted substantially higher force per myosin and greater crossbridge binding. At a high calcium level (pCa 4), the multiple-filament model predicted approximately 2 piconewtons per crossbridge, compared to approximately 0.5 piconewtons for the two-filament model—values that aligned better with data from single-molecule experiments. The key mechanism underlying this difference is compliant realignment: when a crossbridge binds and undergoes its power stroke, it displaces the thin filament relative to the thick filament, bringing neighboring crossbridge heads into more favorable alignment for binding. This cooperative recruitment is amplified as more filaments interact, because each binding event affects a larger mechanical neighborhood.


Extensions to the Spatially Explicit Framework
Several groups have extended these spatially explicit models in different directions. Some models have added titin as a passive spring element connecting the free end of the myosin to the Z disk, showing that titin has a significant effect on passive force as sarcomere length changes. Others have incorporated myosin binding protein C (located in the C zone of the thick filament), which competes with actin binding—reducing crossbridge availability—through a kinetic scheme that represents its stabilizing effect on the myosin head. Additional work has addressed the three-dimensional nature of crossbridge motion, since crossbridges undergo both a longitudinal (along-filament) displacement and a torsional or transverse component during the power stroke, with implications for lattice spacing as muscle length changes. One group has also used spatially explicit frameworks to simulate muscle twitches and work loops, allowing examination of stress, strain, and energy use during dynamic contractions.
Thick filament activation can also in principle be incorporated into this framework by adding a mechanically sensitive transition in the kinetic scheme. In such a formulation, the rate of transition from the super-relaxed state to the disordered-relaxed state—which makes myosin heads available to interact with actin—would depend on local mechanical strain along the thick filament, specifically the stretch of the spring segments between thick filament nodes.


Code Implementation
A MATLAB implementation of the two-filament Monte Carlo model, following the Daniel et al. 1998 framework, is available in the workshop research folder. The main script calls a parameter file (where values such as filament spring constants can be modified), a model-building function that establishes node positions and tracks which crossbridge nodes can interact with which actin binding sites, and a kinetics rate function that evaluates position-dependent attachment and detachment probabilities. The model is run multiple times (e.g., 25 repetitions) and forces are averaged across runs to reduce stochastic variability. Outputs include mean force (in piconewtons) and the fraction of crossbridge heads bound, both plotted as a function of time; an exponential fit extracts the asymptotic force level and the rate constant to half-maximum. Reducing thin filament stiffness to one-tenth of its default value produces slightly less force (because more mechanical energy is absorbed by filament stretching rather than converted to force output) while increasing the fraction of bound crossbridges—illustrating the interplay between filament compliance and force production that motivated this class of models in the first place.


Modeling Disease and Injury
Spatially explicit frameworks can be adapted to address pathological conditions at multiple organizational scales. Molecular-level mutations affecting troponin, tropomyosin, or myosin kinetics—for example, prolonged crossbridge attachment due to impaired detachment—can be simulated by changing kinetic rate functions. Tissue-level changes such as collagen deposition during injury recovery can be incorporated as modified passive mechanical elements, analogous to the parallel passive element in the Hill model.


Principles of Model Selection
A central principle in computational muscle modeling is that the model must include a parameter or subsystem representing the process being studied: if there is no control knob for the variable of interest, the model cannot answer the question. The key practical challenge is deciding how much detail to include, since incorporating full spatial detail greatly increases computational cost.
