title: So you want to simulate movement?
text:
Overview

Why Simulate Movement?
Computer simulation of locomotion complements physical experiments by enabling researchers to test hypotheses and explore conditions that would be impossible or unethical to impose on live animals. Simulation also bridges experimental biology and robotics: the same mathematical models that capture animal locomotion dynamics can serve as the basis for bio-inspired control of robotic systems.


Math Models Come in Many Forms
Mathematical models of movement range from highly detailed musculoskeletal models — such as those built in OpenSim, a platform downloaded hundreds of thousands of times — to simple reduced-order models that capture essential dynamics with very few parameters. A spring-loaded inverted pendulum (SLIP) model, for example, has been used to examine how animals maintain stability when stepping into unexpected obstacles, recovering realistic locomotor behavior from a minimal representation. Simple models are also central to bio-inspired robotics, where animal-like movement can emerge as a consequence of optimizing control within a reduced-order model.


Dynamical Systems and Differential Equations
A dynamical system is one whose behavior changes over time, described by differential equations that relate state variables to their time derivatives. Simple systems such as exponential population growth (dP/dt = αP) have exact analytical solutions (P(t) = Ce^(αt)); others, such as the nonlinear pendulum (d²θ/dt² = −(g/L)sin(θ)), do not admit solutions in terms of elementary functions and must be solved numerically. Numerical simulation is therefore necessary for most practical models of movement.


Euler’s Method: Numerical Approximation
Euler’s method is the simplest numerical approach to solving ordinary differential equations, derived from the definition of a derivative: X(t+Δt) ≈ X(t) + (dX/dt)·Δt. By repeatedly applying this update rule with a small time step Δt, the simulation steps the system forward through time. Accuracy depends critically on Δt: too large a step causes energy drift in conservative systems, while a sufficiently small step produces results consistent with analytical solutions.


State Variables and Systems of First-Order ODEs
Euler’s method applies directly to first-order ordinary differential equations, but mechanical systems governed by Newton’s second law (F = ma) typically involve second-order equations. By defining both position and velocity as separate state variables, a second-order equation of motion can be rewritten as two coupled first-order ODEs, making Euler’s method (and other numerical integrators) directly applicable. The state vector must contain exactly the information needed to propagate the system forward: for a moving mass, that is its current position and velocity.


Simulating the 1D Spring-Loaded Inverted Pendulum in MATLAB
A one-dimensional SLIP model consists of a point mass on a spring under gravity; summing forces gives the equation of motion MZ̈ = −Mg + K(L₀ − Z), which converts to two coupled first-order ODEs in position Z and velocity dZ/dt. Euler’s method can be implemented in MATLAB as a for loop with pre-allocated output arrays for efficiency; MATLAB’s built-in ode45 solver provides a more accurate alternative by automatically adapting the time step through comparison of 4th- and 5th-order Runge-Kutta integration steps.


Hybrid Dynamics and Liftoff
Many locomotion models are hybrid dynamical systems: the governing equations switch between different forms depending on the phase of motion. In a hopping SLIP model, the stance phase applies both gravity and spring force, while the flight phase applies gravity alone; the transition from stance to flight occurs when the spring passes its natural length L₀, because the ground can only push upward and cannot pull the foot downward. MATLAB’s ode45 event detection feature can identify the precise moment of liftoff or touchdown, enabling more accurate handling of these phase transitions than a simple conditional check within a fixed-step loop.

title: Using motion capture and electromyography (EMG) in movement sciences
text:
Overview

Inverse Kinematics: Estimating Joint Angles
Inverse kinematics estimates joint angles from limited positional information — for example, at joint centers with no directly accessible bony landmark, or in animal models where marker placement is constrained. Given known segment lengths and the position of one endpoint, a system of equations derived from the law of cosines can recover the intermediate joint angles; biological constraints on anatomical range of motion resolve the sign ambiguity that arises when taking an arc cosine. The technique underlies all commercial motion capture software, is used internally by markerless systems to constrain pose estimates to anatomically plausible configurations, and is applied by gap-filling algorithms when a reflective marker is occluded during a trial.


Inverse Dynamics: Computing Joint Moments
Inverse dynamics extends kinematic data to estimate net joint moments by incorporating external force information. The bottom-up approach begins with ground reaction forces measured by a force plate and works segment-by-segment toward the joints of interest, computing moments from the cross product of each force vector and its moment arm. The complementary top-down approach starts from a segment with a known external force — such as a limb in swing phase or the head — and works downward; software such as OpenSim uses both approaches simultaneously, treating the difference between them as a data-quality indicator.


Best Practices for Motion Capture Data Collection
Motion capture is a sequential processing pipeline — marker placement, triangulation, model building, variable computation — so errors at any early stage propagate and compound through all later steps. Markers are placed on bony landmarks to minimize soft tissue artifact, the displacement of a marker caused by overlying skin or muscle shifting relative to the underlying bone during movement. Practical safeguards include using tight-fitting clothing, calibrating the system before each data collection session, continuously monitoring marker trajectories during trials, and re-collecting any questionable trial immediately rather than attempting repair during processing.


How EMG Works: Bipolar Electrodes and Signal Generation
Surface electromyography records the summed electrical activity of multiple motor units in the underlying muscle. Each motor unit action potential is triggered at the neuromuscular junction — where acetylcholine release changes fiber membrane permeability — and propagates along the muscle fiber as a wave of depolarization that is detected as a voltage difference between a bipolar electrode’s two sites. The electrodes must be oriented parallel to the muscle fiber direction and must not straddle the neuromuscular junction, where simultaneous activation of both sites would cancel the differential signal; in animal models, fine wire electrodes — insulated twisted-pair wires with bare tips — are inserted via hypodermic needle for intramuscular recording.


Best Practices for EMG Data Collection
Reliable surface EMG depends on correct anatomical electrode placement, confirmed by palpating the target muscle during voluntary contraction before attaching the sensor. Skin preparation — light exfoliation followed by alcohol cleaning — reduces impedance at the electrode–skin interface, and electrodes should be secured against movement artifact and verified against the recording software before data collection begins. Published placement guidelines such as SENIAM provide anatomical starting points but should be adapted to individual anatomy; for fine wire electrodes in animal preparations, conductivity and insulation integrity must be confirmed with a multimeter before insertion.


EMG Signal Processing: From Raw Signal to Envelope
The standard surface EMG processing pipeline applies a high-pass filter (typically 20–30 Hz) to remove DC offset and low-frequency motion artifact, followed by full-wave rectification (taking the absolute value of each sample), and then a low-pass filter (typically 10–20 Hz) to smooth the result into the linear activation envelope most commonly shown in published figures. Fast Fourier transformation (FFT) of the raw signal is a useful diagnostic step that converts the signal into the frequency domain, revealing noise sources — such as 50 or 60 Hz AC electrical interference — that may warrant a targeted notch filter. Signal decomposition, which uses electrode arrays and specialized algorithms to resolve individual motor unit action potential trains, offers greater mechanistic insight but requires two-dimensional or intramuscular electrode configurations not available with standard bipolar surface electrodes.

title: Modeling the muscle spindle
text:
Overview

Anatomy and function of the muscle spindle
The muscle spindle is a mechanosensory organ embedded in parallel with extrafusal muscle fibers, containing three types of intrafusal fibers — bag 1, bag 2, and chain — grouped here into two functional populations (bag and chain) based on the similar mechanical properties of bag 2 and chain fibers. Two afferent pathways relay spindle signals to the central nervous system: the primary 1A afferent, which reads from both bag and chain fibers, and the group 2 afferent, which connects only to chain fibers; the 1A afferent is the focus of this model. Unlike most sensory organs, the spindle receives its own motor drive: gamma dynamic motor neurons project to bag fibers and gamma static motor neurons to chain fibers, allowing the central nervous system to modulate spindle sensitivity independently of extrafusal muscle activation via alpha motor neurons.


History dependence of spindle firing
The 1A afferent exhibits history-dependent firing: an initial stretch of a resting spindle produces a high-frequency burst, but a subsequent stretch of the same amplitude does not reproduce that burst once the spindle has been previously stretched. This property parallels history dependence in extrafusal muscle force, where cross-bridge dynamics are the accepted mechanistic explanation, and the same mechanism is hypothesized to govern intrafusal fiber behavior. The biophysical model presented here is built on that cross-bridge premise, applying separate parameter sets to extrafusal, bag, and chain fibers to capture their distinct mechanical properties.


Model architecture and biophysics
Model inputs are muscle tendon unit (MTU) length, alpha motor activation, and gamma motor activations (dynamic and static); because intrafusal fibers are in parallel with the fascicle rather than the full MTU, the model first solves a force balance between fascicle and tendon to obtain fascicle length, which varies with alpha activation-dependent fascicle stiffness. Cross-bridge mechanics compute force in each intrafusal fiber type; yank (the rate of change of force) is computed from the bag fiber only, with negative values discarded by half-wave rectification, and a weighted sum of force and rectified yank produces the receptor potential. The receptor potential is converted to firing rate via an integrate-and-fire function running at a 1 ms time step, imposing a ceiling of 250 spikes per second, though the tutorial interface outputs receptor potential directly to allow wider parameter exploration without hitting that ceiling.


Using the model: forward simulation and optimization
The model requires MATLAB 2020A or later with the Signal Processing Toolbox, and accepts MTU length (or fascicle length directly), alpha activation, and gamma motor activations as inputs for forward simulation. Because gamma motor activity is rarely measured directly in experiments, an optimization mode is provided: the user supplies a measured 1A afferent firing record and the optimizer — using either a gradient-based solver (fmincon) or a gradient-free alternative (pattern search) — iteratively estimates the gamma activations that best reproduce that record. Model parameters were derived from optical and molecular characterization of intrafusal fibers and electrophysiological recordings from anesthetized animals; direct mechanical testing of intrafusal fibers has not been performed due to their small size, so parameter estimates rely on indirect characterization.

title: Best practices for scientific programming
text:
Overview

Why Programming Practices Matter in Science
Good programming practices matter because scientific work can be elegant but fragile when built on weak foundations — a “house of cards” that can collapse at a critical moment. Two recurring failure modes illustrate this risk. The first occurs when a researcher submits a paper, receives reviewer feedback months later requesting reanalysis, and finds their files too disorganized to work with efficiently. The second occurs when a student defends or leaves a lab and the remaining data and code are difficult for anyone else to use. The practices described in this workshop are directly motivated by these kinds of failures.


Phases of a Programming Workflow
Scientific programming involves two broad phases. The first is a prototyping phase, in which the goal is to explore data and get things working quickly — adding test cases and analyses to a single script, reusing existing code, and accepting something that works for the moment. The second is a development phase, in which code is refined to be robust, well-documented, and shareable. Researchers often remain in the prototyping phase indefinitely; a key discipline is knowing when and how to transition to higher-quality code. A third phase — sharing work publicly — is also important: data funded by public money should ultimately be made available to the community, but this requires adequate documentation and archiving.


Documenting Your Experimental Protocol
Before data collection begins, write a detailed experimental protocol in a Word document or Google Doc. The protocol should list every step of the experiment, including verbatim instructions given to participants, consent procedures, and screenshots of relevant software settings. A protocol can never be too detailed. The goal is that a new lab member, already familiar with basic equipment, should be able to follow the protocol step by step without additional guidance. Having another student attempt to execute a new protocol is a reliable way to identify steps that are not well defined.


File Organization and Naming Conventions
Define a folder structure for each study before data collection begins. A typical structure includes separate folders for individual subjects, group data, analysis scripts, and papers or presentations. Once the structure is defined, apply it consistently across all participants. File names should be machine-readable: no spaces, consistent capitalization, and a consistent number of digits for numerical IDs. Without leading zeros, a file system will sort “subject11” before “subject2” because it compares character by character. For date stamps, use year-month-day format with 24-hour time. Participant names or initials must never appear in file names: this would make the data identifiable and render it no longer HIPAA compliant.


Metadata, README Files, and Off-Boarding
Supporting documentation — referred to as metadata — should accompany all data. Plain-text README files should describe variable coding, units, omitted items in clinical assessments, and other details that cannot easily be embedded in standard data files. Well-maintained metadata allow a researcher to return to data collected years earlier and get up to speed quickly. An off-boarding checklist is a practical way to enforce these standards in a lab setting: graduating students organize all physical documents (consent forms, data collection sheets), digital data, experiment code, and analysis scripts, and review them with the principal investigator before dissertation defense sign-off. Treating this review as a requirement for graduation helps ensure that data and code remain usable after a student leaves.


Knowing Your Data
Before writing analysis code, develop a clear understanding of four aspects of your data: how the data were collected (protocol, hardware, and any factors that might influence data properties); the sampling frequency, especially for time-series data such as force, EMG, or marker position; the units of each variable (confusion between meters and millimeters, or degrees and radians, is a common and consequential error); and the file format. Interoperable formats — CSV, Excel, and JSON — can be read across programming languages and statistical software. Proprietary formats such as MATLAB’s MAT files and motion-capture C3D files may not be readable outside their native software.


Building a Data Analysis Pipeline
A well-designed data analysis pipeline moves from data import through quality control, preprocessing, computation of summary measures, figure creation, and statistical analysis. The bulk of these steps should be automated rather than executed manually. A four-script MATLAB pipeline illustrates this structure: scripts are numbered to indicate run order and named with action verbs — simulate data, combine data, summarize data, and create figures. Analyzing the first participant’s complete dataset before collecting all participants’ data is a valuable step, because it frequently reveals weaknesses or gaps in the pipeline that can be corrected before large-scale data collection begins.
The majority of the movement science and biomechanics community uses MATLAB, while researchers in neuroimaging have largely moved to Python. MATLAB is relatively easy to teach and has centralized, well-organized documentation. Regardless of which language is used for analysis, data can be exported as CSV or plain-text files, making data sharing possible across communities even when code cannot be directly reused.


Writing Readable and Reusable Code
Several practices improve code readability and reusability. Avoid single-letter variable names such as x, y, i, or j; instead, choose names that reflect what the variable represents — for example, naming a loop variable “participant” rather than “i” when cycling through participants. Break complex operations across multiple lines rather than writing long single-line expressions. Avoid copying and pasting code blocks and changing variable names: this practice increases the probability of introducing hard-to-detect errors, because the code will run and may produce a plausible result even when a name has been missed. The recommended alternative is to write functions. MATLAB includes a refactoring feature that converts selected lines of code into a local function by right-clicking and selecting “convert to a local function.” A local function is appropriate when the operation is unlikely to be needed in other scripts; if the function may be reused across projects, it should be saved as a separate function file.


Verifying Code Correctness
A lack of error messages does not guarantee correct results. A common illustration of this is a script that plots the same variable on both axes of a figure: the script produces no errors and the result looks plausible (an upward trend), but the figure is wrong — once the correct variable is placed on the y-axis, the trend disappears. Unit testing is a formal way to verify correctness: test code supplies known inputs to a function and checks whether the output matches the expected value. MATLAB provides a tutorial course on unit testing. For version control, the simplest approach is to save a working script under a new name before making changes, so that the prior version is preserved. GitHub is a more formal tool for version control and code sharing.

title: Material properties in biomechanics
text:
Overview

Introduction: From Frog Tongues to Muscle Mechanics
Standard treatments of biomechanics material properties emphasize bone, cartilage, and tendon, but skeletal muscle is itself a material with distinctive and tunable mechanical properties. Projectile-tongue feeding in frogs and toads provides a vivid example of demanding energy requirements: the jaw-opening muscles reach maximum length when the mouth is closed, precluding active pre-stretch, yet must store and release energy at very high rates to capture fast-moving prey. Understanding where and how muscles store elastic energy — and how activation modifies that storage — is the central question addressed in this module.


Springs, Dampers, and the Foundations of Viscoelasticity
A linear spring obeys Hooke’s Law: force is proportional to displacement (F = kx), or in normalized form, stress equals elastic modulus times strain (σ = Eε). A damper (dashpot) generates force proportional to the rate of displacement rather than displacement itself (F = bẋ, where b is the damping constant). Both spring and damper properties scale consistently from the whole-muscle level down to individual filaments within the sarcomere, because they depend on material composition rather than specimen size.


Viscoelastic Models: From Two to Four Elements
Combining springs and dampers in different arrangements produces viscoelastic models with distinct force-time behaviors. The Maxwell model (spring and damper in series) produces an initial large force that decays to zero under a fixed strain; the Kelvin-Voigt model (spring and damper in parallel) produces a force that decays only to the residual elastic force in the spring. The Hill model places a spring in series with a Kelvin-Voigt element; the time constant τ = b/E of a Kelvin-Voigt element governs how quickly force decays after a perturbation, and more complex multi-element arrangements produce correspondingly richer behaviors.


Measuring Viscoelastic Properties: Three Experimental Approaches
Three experimental protocols are commonly used to characterize viscoelastic properties in muscle: ramp stretch-and-hold, sinusoidal perturbations, and white-noise perturbations. Sinusoidal protocols allow elastic and viscous contributions to be decomposed because elastic forces are in phase with the oscillation while viscous forces are 90 degrees out of phase; white-noise protocols probe multiple frequencies simultaneously and can reduce total experiment time. Kirsch, Boskov, and Rymer (1994, IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering) compared all three protocols in cat soleus and found that no single standard model fit both ramp-stretch and white-noise data simultaneously, with best-fitting models explaining only 80–85% of force variance.


System Identification in Mouse and Frog Muscles
Ramp-stretch experiments performed across the full physiological range of muscle lengths — both passively and at the plateau of isometric force — combined with system identification reveal the structure of the best-fitting viscoelastic model of muscle. A model consisting of two Kelvin-Voigt elements in series fits data from mouse soleus and three bullfrog muscles (sartorius, iliofibularis, semitendinosus) with high R-squared values and residuals on the order of 10⁻⁴. Comparison across three titin genotypes of mouse soleus — wild type, the Mdm spontaneous mutant (deletion of ~50 amino acids at the N2A/PEVK boundary), and a transgenic with exons 112–158 of PEVK titin deleted — provides independent evidence that titin structure drives differences between the two model elements.


Titin Subdomain Assignment and Activation-Dependent Tuning
The two Kelvin-Voigt elements identified by system identification (k1/b1 and k2/b2) differ in passive behavior and response to activation, pointing to distinct molecular origins within titin. The k1/b1 element, assigned to the PEVK1 and PEVK2 sub-domains near the Z-disc, behaves as an exponential spring whose stiffness varies over approximately three orders of magnitude across physiological length; upon activation, its time constant increases from ~100 ms to ~0.5–1 s, enabling energy retention across a full locomotor cycle. The k2/b2 element, assigned to the PEVK3 sub-domain near the M-line, stiffens and transitions from exponential to linear spring behavior upon activation while its time constant shortens to ~5 ms. This contrasting behavior means activation shifts energy storage predominantly into the slower k1/b1 element, dramatically extending the timescale over which elastic energy is retained relative to passive muscle.


Power, Energy Storage, and Comparison to Prior Literature
Elastic energy stored in each Kelvin-Voigt element can be estimated from system-identified stiffness values as ½kx² (equivalently ½F²/k), with approximately two-thirds of stored energy dissipating within one time constant. For frog sartorius, total power in the viscoelastic transmission rises from ~1 W/kg passively to ~100 W/kg upon activation; for semitendinosus, from ~8 W/kg to ~200 W/kg. Energy stored in active frog sartorius reaches approximately 0.063 P₀L₀, close to the 0.092 P₀L₀ total storage reported by Linari, Woledge, and Curtin (2003, Journal of Physiology) from single frog anterior tibialis fibers — work that found only approximately one-third of stored energy explicable by cross-bridges, thick filaments, thin filaments, and tendons combined.


Broader Implications and Extensions
Skeletal muscle functions as a tunable viscoelastic actuator that can harvest energy from environmental loads during stretch and release stored energy to amplify or redirect cross-bridge power output, with individual titin domains specialized for mechanical roles spanning orders of magnitude in frequency and force. The two-Kelvin-Voigt model is planned for extension to muscle-tendon units by adding a series spring representing the external tendon, and differences between fast and slow muscles in titin N2A actin-binding site location (closer to the Z-disc in EDL than in soleus) have been characterized as a fast-muscle high-gear configuration. Open-source Lagrangian dynamics models incorporating cross-bridge activation, N2A actin-binding dynamics, thin-filament titin winding, and length- and activation-dependent viscoelasticity are under development as replacements for Hill models in musculoskeletal simulations.

title: Movement exploration
text:
Overview

Measuring functional mobility
The Timed Up and Go (TUG) test is a widely used clinical measure of functional mobility in which a participant rises from a chair, walks 3 metres, turns, and returns to sitting. Like many standardised functional scales, the TUG and related balance assessments can exhibit ceiling and floor effects across populations with widely varying capacity, reducing sensitivity at the extremes of ability and limiting their usefulness as outcome measures in heterogeneous samples.


Markerless pose estimation
Markerless pose estimation tools extract joint positions from standard video without attaching physical markers to participants, extending kinematic data collection to clinical and naturalistic settings. AlphaPose uses regional multi-person detection to locate body keypoints in video frames; DeepLabCut, originally developed for animal behaviour research, applies deep learning to track user-defined landmarks and has since been validated for human biomechanics applications. Both tools substantially lower the logistical barrier to movement data collection outside a traditional motion-capture laboratory.


Psychophysiological measures and movement-related anxiety
Electrodermal activity (EDA), or skin conductance, reflects sympathetic nervous system arousal and is used as a physiological index of anxiety in studies of motor behaviour. A related clinical construct is kinesiophobia — fear of movement resulting from perceived vulnerability to painful re-injury — which can cause patients to avoid beneficial movement even after tissue recovery, prolonging disability beyond what physical damage alone would predict.


Virtual reality as a research tool for anxiety induction
Studying how anxiety affects gait and balance requires inducing a sense of threat without exposing participants to genuine fall risk. Height-simulating virtual reality environments provide a controlled alternative, allowing systematic manipulation of perceived threat level while maintaining physical safety and enabling investigators to measure how anxiety-related physiological and behavioural changes interact with postural control and locomotion.

title: Introduction to x-ray diffraction
text:
Overview

Why molecular-scale measurements matter in muscle biology
Muscle is hierarchically organized from the whole organ down to individual protein filaments; at the sarcomere level, the interdigitating arrays of thick (myosin) and thin (actin) filaments span roughly 1–10 micrometers, a length scale conserved across species from cockroaches to blue whales. Around 1666, Jan Swammerdam demonstrated that muscle volume does not change during contraction by placing a frog muscle in a sealed, fluid-filled chamber with a capillary indicator — stimulating the nerve produced no indicator movement, disproving the prevailing hypothesis that nerve fluid inflated the muscle (Cobb, M., 2002, Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 3, 395–400. DOI: 10.1038/nrn806). When a muscle shortens, the hexagonal lattice of filaments must expand radially; because filament-to-filament spacings are tens of nanometers, they fall well below the resolution of light microscopy and cannot be measured in living muscle by electron microscopy — X-ray diffraction fills this gap by measuring nanometer-scale lattice parameters in contracting muscle with millisecond time resolution.


What are X-rays and how do they diffract?
X-rays are electromagnetic waves with wavelengths of approximately 0.1–0.2 nm, comparable to atomic-scale distances in biological molecules; when a beam encounters electrons arranged in a regular, repeating structure, constructive interference produces sharp reflections at angles satisfying Bragg’s law: nλ = 2d sinθ, where λ is wavelength, d is the plane spacing, θ is the angle between beam and planes, and n is an integer. In muscle experiments the diffraction angles are very small, allowing the approximation d = λL/S, where L is the sample-to-detector distance and S is the distance from beam center to reflection; reflections closer to the beam center correspond to larger real-space spacings, an inverse relationship called reciprocal space. Franklin & Gosling (1953, Nature, 171, 740–741. DOI: 10.1038/171740a0) showed the power of this approach in DNA; the same physical principles apply to the ordered filament arrays of muscle.


The myofilament lattice as a quasi-crystal
Within each sarcomere, thick and thin filaments form a regular hexagonal lattice repeating across thousands of unit cells in the fiber cross-section — sufficient regularity for coherent diffraction even though muscle is not a perfect crystal. Because myofibrils are randomly rotated around the beam axis, the diffraction pattern is rotationally averaged: reflections appear as arcs rather than discrete spots. The horizontal detector axis (the equator) carries reflections reporting the lateral arrangement of filaments in cross-section, while the vertical axis (the meridian) and off-meridional layer lines carry reflections reporting repeating structures along the filament axis.


Equatorial reflections: reading the cross-sectional lattice
Equatorial reflections arise from repeating planes in the hexagonal lattice labeled by Miller indices (h, k); the I(1,0) and I(1,1) reflections are typically the strongest, and the center-to-center thick filament spacing D10 is calculated from the I(1,0) position using the small-angle Bragg relation — representative values are approximately 40–45 nm for insect and vertebrate muscle under relaxed conditions (Franzini-Armstrong & Peachey, 1981, J Cell Biol, 91, 166s–186s. DOI: 10.1083/jcb.91.3.166s). As myosin heads bind actin during activation, mass transfers radially outward within the unit cell; the I(1,1)/I(1,0) intensity ratio is the standard indicator of cross-bridge attachment in vertebrate muscle: as more heads bind, I(1,0) decreases and I(1,1) increases (Haselgrove & Huxley, 1973, J Mol Biol, 77, 549–568. DOI: 10.1016/0022-2836(73)90222-2; Millman, 1998, Physiol Rev, 78, 359–391. DOI: 10.1152/physrev.1998.78.2.359). Lethocerus — the giant water bug (Order Hemiptera, Family Belostomatidae) — has flight muscle among the most crystalline of any animal specimen ever characterized by this technique, making it the standard specimen for high-resolution insect muscle diffraction since the 1960s (Reedy, 1968, J Mol Biol, 31, 155–176. DOI: 10.1016/0022-2836(68)90437-3).


Meridional reflections and layer lines: axial and helical structure
Myosin heads project from the thick filament in crowns spaced approximately 14.3 nm apart, producing the strong M3 meridional reflection and higher-order reflections M6 and M15; changes in M3 intensity and position during contraction report myosin head displacement and strain in real time (Huxley & Brown, 1967, J Mol Biol, 30, 383–434. DOI: 10.1016/S0022-2836(67)80046-9). F-actin forms a 13/6 helix with a pseudo-repeat of approximately 36.0–36.5 nm, producing off-meridional actin layer lines A6 (pitch ~5.9 nm) and A7 (~5.1 nm) (Holmes et al., 1990, Nature, 347, 44–49. DOI: 10.1038/347044a0). The ~38.5 nm repeat sometimes observed in muscle diffraction is a distinct structural parameter arising from the tropomyosin/troponin regulatory protein repeat, not from the actin helix geometry (Egelman et al., 1982, Nature, 298, 131–135. DOI: 10.1038/298131a0).


Performing experiments at a synchrotron beamline
Conventional laboratory X-ray sources lack the photon flux to observe weak reflections or capture rapid structural changes in contracting muscle; synchrotron facilities overcome this by accelerating electrons near the speed of light and harvesting extremely intense X-ray beams from the resulting radiation. The Advanced Photon Source (APS) at Argonne National Laboratory — home to the BioCAT beamline used for many muscle diffraction experiments — has a storage ring approximately 350 m in diameter; a silicon monochromator selects a single wavelength, and the resulting focused beam passes through a hydrated muscle specimen to a detector placed 3–5 m away. Modern synchrotron detectors record complete diffraction patterns at millisecond time resolution, fast enough to follow structural changes through a single twitch contraction, while simultaneous force transducers record mechanical output for direct comparison with molecular structural changes.


From molecular structure to whole-muscle function: a case study
Two cockroach leg muscles — numbered 178 and 179 — act on the same joint, share a single motor neuron, and have identical mass, moment arm, and force-length and force-velocity curves, yet work loop experiments show that one produces net positive work (a motor) while the other absorbs net energy (a brake) — a functional distinction first characterized by Ahn & Full (2002, J Exp Biol, 205, 379–389. DOI: 10.1242/jeb.205.3.379). Time-resolved synchrotron X-ray diffraction at the APS beamline identified differences in myofilament lattice structure between the two muscles that were invisible to conventional mechanical assays, and spatially explicit computational models incorporating lattice geometry can qualitatively reproduce the different work loop shapes from muscles with otherwise identical cross-bridge kinetics. This example illustrates the unique capability of time-resolved X-ray diffraction: detecting structural differences that operate at the length and time scales where molecular mechanisms determine whole-muscle function.

title: Introduction to muscle anatomy and physiology
text:
Overview

The Conserved and Versatile Muscular System
The muscular system is one of the most highly conserved across the animal kingdom, with the fundamental organization of muscle, mechanisms of force generation, and responses to activation shared from insects to large mammals (Burkholder & Lieber, 2001). Despite this conservation, muscles are functionally versatile: a single muscle can act as a motor generating mechanical work, a spring storing and returning elastic energy, a brake absorbing energy during active lengthening, or a strut transmitting force with minimal length change. Subtle differences in structure, protein isoform expression, architecture, or neural control can substantially alter whole-animal performance.


Sarcomere Structure and Hierarchical Organization
Skeletal muscle is organized hierarchically: the whole muscle comprises fascicles containing individual fibers, each fiber contains myofibrils, and each myofibril consists of repeating contractile units called sarcomeres. The sarcomere—bounded by Z-discs, with thin actin filaments extending inward and thick myosin filaments anchored at the M-line—is the fundamental unit of force generation; resting sarcomere length in vertebrates is typically 2.0–2.5 µm (Gordon et al., 1966; Burkholder & Lieber, 2001). A third filament, titin, spans from the Z-disc to the M-line and provides passive elastic resistance when the sarcomere is stretched (Labeit & Kolmerer, 1995). Invertebrate sarcomeres can differ substantially: obliquely striated muscle found in some soft-bodied animals can elongate far beyond the range of vertebrate sarcomeres while still generating force, a property called superelongation (Rosenbluth, 1967).


Excitation-Contraction Coupling
Excitation-contraction coupling (ECC) links an action potential at the muscle membrane to mechanical contraction: the action potential propagates into the T-tubule network, triggering calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum through ryanodine receptor channels, and the resulting rise in intracellular calcium causes troponin to expose myosin-binding sites on actin (Bers, 2002). Relaxation requires calcium to be pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum by SERCA, an energy-requiring process that is slower than calcium release; this kinetic asymmetry allows successive stimuli to sum when they arrive before full relaxation—a process called temporal summation. ECC kinetics vary across fiber types: muscles that operate at high contraction frequencies have higher sarcoplasmic reticulum density and faster calcium cycling machinery than slow-twitch fibers (Berchtold et al., 2000).


Force-Frequency Relationship
Force output increases with stimulation frequency as successive twitches overlap before the muscle fully relaxes—a process called summation—culminating in fused tetanus, where force is smooth and maximal, when twitches overlap completely (Lieber, 2002). This relationship arises from calcium dynamics: higher frequencies allow calcium to accumulate in the cytoplasm, activating more cross-bridges and increasing force until a ceiling set by cross-bridge number and sarcomere geometry is reached. In intact animals, the nervous system modulates both stimulation frequency (rate coding) and motor unit recruitment to produce graded forces, and brief high-frequency bursts (doublet potentiation) can transiently enhance force beyond what steady-state measurements predict.


Force-Length Relationship
Active muscle force peaks at the optimal length (L₀), where cross-bridge overlap between thick and thin filaments is greatest, and declines at both shorter lengths (steric interference between filaments) and longer lengths (reduced overlap), following the classic Gordon-Huxley-Julian force-length curve (Gordon et al., 1966). Passive force, contributed primarily by titin and the extracellular matrix, increases progressively with length, so total muscle force at any length is the sum of active and passive contributions. Operating range varies across species: most vertebrate muscles function near the descending limb during natural movements, while some invertebrate muscles—including proposed super-contracting chameleon tongue retractor muscles—maintain force at sarcomere lengths far outside the vertebrate range (Herrel et al., 2001). The force-length relationship is a quasi-static, isometric measure; active stretching and shortening during natural movements can cause force to deviate substantially from this curve.


Force-Velocity Relationship and Muscle Architecture
Active force during shortening decreases with increasing velocity—the force-velocity relationship—reaching maximum at isometric conditions and falling to zero at maximum shortening velocity (V_max), a relationship reflecting cross-bridge cycling kinetics first characterized by Hill (1938). Power output—the product of force and velocity—peaks at approximately one-third of V_max in many vertebrate muscles and declines toward both extremes (Josephson, 1993); fast-twitch fibers achieve higher peak power than slow-twitch fibers because of their faster myosin ATPase activity and cross-bridge cycling rate. Muscle architecture—the arrangement of fibers relative to the line of action—determines the force and velocity characteristics of the whole muscle: parallel-fibered muscles maximize shortening speed and excursion by placing more sarcomeres in series, while pennate muscles pack more fibers into a given volume, increasing physiological cross-sectional area and maximum force capacity at some cost to shortening velocity (Lieber & Fridén, 2000). The force-velocity relationship is measured under isotonic, maximal-activation conditions and does not capture history-dependent effects, submaximal activation, or contributions from elastic structures such as titin.


Titin as a Tunable Viscoelastic Spring
Titin is the largest known protein, spanning continuously from the Z-disc to the M-line, and functions as the primary passive elastic element of the sarcomere (Labeit & Kolmerer, 1995). The extensible I-band region contains two mechanically distinct spring segments: a tandem immunoglobulin (Ig) domain region that is compliant at low forces and a PEVK domain that contributes the steeper, exponential rise in passive force at longer sarcomere lengths (Granzier & Labeit, 2004); both regions are sites of alternative splicing that generate isoforms of different lengths and stiffnesses, with longer isoforms (e.g., soleus) conferring lower passive stiffness and shorter isoforms (e.g., psoas) conferring higher stiffness. Evidence from in vitro experiments supports the hypothesis that the N2A element of titin can interact with actin in a calcium-dependent manner, potentially stiffening the sarcomere during active contraction and contributing to force during active stretch—a mechanism under active investigation that is not yet universally accepted (Dutta et al., 2018; Nishikawa, 2020). In invertebrates such as Drosophila, mechanical diversity is generated not through alternative splicing of a single titin gene but through expression of multiple distinct titin-like proteins, including projectin and sallimus (Burkart et al., 2007; Bullard et al., 2005).
