title: System identification
text:
Overview

What Is System Identification?
Mathematical modeling in biomechanics follows two broad paradigms: first-principles modeling derives governing equations from fundamental physical laws with every parameter physically interpretable, while system identification builds mathematical models of dynamical systems from experimentally measured input-output data. System identification models serve three main purposes: characterizing and analyzing system behavior, predicting system outputs from a given input, and designing controllers that interact with the system. Models occupy a spectrum from white-box (high structural fidelity, parameters physically interpretable) through gray-box (known structure with data-driven parameter estimation) to black-box (minimal structural assumptions); research on muscle and tendon mechanics typically employs gray- and white-box approaches, where the model topology is informed by physical intuition and parameters are identified from experiment. The System Identification Toolbox in MATLAB, developed by Lennart Ljung, is the primary computational platform for these analyses; specialized code written by Rick Castler adapts these tools to ramp stretch and transfer-function analyses of muscle and tendon.


Mathematical Foundations: Laplace Transforms and Transfer Functions
The equations governing viscoelastic systems are ordinary differential equations (ODEs) in time; the Laplace transform converts these to algebraic equations by replacing time-derivative operations with multiplication by the complex variable s, greatly simplifying analysis. For a linear system with zero initial conditions, the ratio of output to input in the Laplace domain defines the transfer function — a rational polynomial in s whose numerator roots (zeros) and denominator roots (poles) together determine the system’s frequency response, transient behavior, and stability. Model selection among candidate topologies is guided by goodness-of-fit metrics (R², RMSE) and complexity-penalizing information criteria (Akaike Information Criterion, AIC; Bayesian Information Criterion, BIC), which guard against overfitting by penalizing unnecessary model complexity.


Viscoelastic Building Blocks: Springs, Dampers, and Their Combinations
A linear spring produces force proportional to displacement (F = kx) and is a static model, while a linear damper produces force proportional to velocity (F = Bẋ) and is a dynamic model. These elements combine into canonical two-element models: the Maxwell model (spring in series with a damper) cannot sustain a static force and behaves as a fluid, whereas the Kelvin-Voigt model (spring in parallel with a damper) sustains a static force and behaves as a solid with time constant τ = B/k. Across multiple species and preparations, skeletal muscle (cat soleus, frog sartorius and semitendinosus, rat medial gastrocnemius, and a range of mouse muscles) is consistently described by two Kelvin-Voigt elements in series, while tendon (rat tail) is described by a Kelvin-Voigt solid.


Experimental Identification of Viscoelastic Models
Three experimental protocols probe viscoelastic properties using length as input and force as output: ramp stretch and hold (transient force spike and subsequent relaxation), sinusoidal perturbation (elastic components respond in phase, viscous components out of phase), and white-noise pseudorandom perturbation (broadband frequency coverage). All three protocols yield equivalent parameter estimates in principle; ramp stretch is most similar to in vivo perturbations and allows systematic sampling across the physiological length range (approximately 0.8 to 1.2 times optimal length) with minimal fatigue. Parameters are estimated by minimizing the sum of squared error between the model response and experimental measurements using least-squares methods in MATLAB’s System Identification Toolbox. Passive muscles display a Kelvin-Voigt-like force response (spike followed by exponential decay), while active muscles produce a larger initial force and slower decay, with the second Kelvin-Voigt element (KV2) becoming substantially stiffer upon stimulation and concentrating nearly all elastic energy storage in the first element (KV1).


Energy Storage, Power Amplification, and Dissipation
Once spring constants k and damping coefficients B are identified, energy stored (E = ½kx²), power (P = F × v), and time constant (τ = B/k) follow analytically for each element. Because the two Kelvin-Voigt elements in the muscle model are in series and share the same force, the element with the lower spring constant stores more energy; upon activation, KV2 stiffens markedly and nearly all elastic energy concentrates in KV1, with KV2 functioning primarily as a mechanical brake. Linari and colleagues (2003) measured heat and work in single frog muscle fibers and found that cross-bridges, internal connective tissue, and filament compliance together could explain only a portion of total stored energy; active-muscle energy values obtained by system identification, expressed in the same P₀ · L₀ units, correspond closely to this previously unexplained fraction, suggesting that active titin viscoelasticity accounts for the remainder.


From Isolated Muscles to Whole-Animal Locomotion
In vivo recordings from guinea fowl running over unexpected obstacles show that during an unexpected step into a hole, muscle force is substantially lower than during a level stride despite a larger EMG signal — and the reverse occurs when stepping up — with both responses occurring faster than neural feedback can operate. These observations implicate the intrinsic mechanical properties of the muscle-tendon unit, particularly titin viscoelasticity, as an automatic stabilization mechanism. The viscoelastic framework also offers a mechanistic explanation for residual force enhancement — the sustained post-stretch force elevation beyond cross-bridge model predictions — as a property of titin rather than cross-bridge cycling.


Connecting Model Elements to Titin Biology
The two Kelvin-Voigt elements identified by system identification correspond to specific domains of titin, the giant elastic protein spanning the half-sarcomere from Z disc to M-line. The PEVK domain — a proline, glutamate, valine, and lysine-rich disordered segment — is the primary structural candidate: a transgenic mouse with a large PEVK deletion shows only a single Kelvin-Voigt element in series with a spring, and passive muscle spring constants change approximately 1,000-fold across the physiological length range (0.8 to 1.2 L₀), consistent with titin’s known exponential spring behavior. Isoform-specific N2 insertions (N2A in most skeletal muscles, N2B in cardiac titin, N2BA in some slow preparations) modulate effective spring length and stiffness, predicting and explaining isoform-dependent variation in viscoelastic parameters identified across frog (sartorius, iliofibularis, semitendinosus), rodent, and cat muscles.

title: Intro to the mechanics of the musculoskeletal system
text:
Overview

Mechanics and its divisions
Mechanics is the study of how bodies respond to applied forces, and divides into two major branches relevant to the musculoskeletal system. In statics, forces are balanced and bodies remain in equilibrium with zero velocity and acceleration; in dynamics, unbalanced forces produce acceleration. Dynamics is further divided into kinematics — describing motion geometry (position, velocity, acceleration) without reference to its causes — and kinetics, which incorporates the forces responsible for motion.


Body segments, joints, and degrees of freedom
The human body is usefully modeled as a system of rigid segments connected at joints, each with its own center of mass and inertia. Degrees of freedom (DOF) define the number of independent motions permitted between two adjacent segments; joints constrain certain DOF and generate reaction forces and moments in constrained directions, which appear as unknowns in free-body-diagram equilibrium analyses. The hip is a ball-and-socket joint with 3 rotational DOF; the humeroulnar articulation of the elbow approximates a hinge with 1 DOF; and the wrist has 2 DOF (flexion/extension and radial/ulnar deviation).


Internal loads and stress states
When external loads act on a body segment, internal loads develop within the structure and can be revealed by cutting a cross-section and applying equilibrium. Normal forces produce tension or compression distributed uniformly across the section; bending moments create a linear stress distribution from maximum tension on one face to maximum compression on the other, with zero stress at the neutral axis; torsional moments produce shear stress greatest at the outer surface and approaching zero at the center. Stress (σ = F/A) and strain (ε = ΔL/L₀) normalize force and deformation by area and original length, respectively, allowing material behavior to be characterized independently of specimen geometry.


Material properties of musculoskeletal tissues
In the linear elastic region, stress and strain are proportional through Young’s modulus E (σ = Eε), where a higher modulus indicates a stiffer material. Musculoskeletal connective tissues display a characteristic nonlinear stress-strain curve progressing through a low-stiffness toe region, a linear elastic region, a yield and micro-failure region, and ultimate failure. Biological tissues differ from idealized elastic solids through anisotropy (properties vary with loading direction due to collagen fiber alignment) and viscoelasticity (stiffness depends on loading rate, with associated creep, stress relaxation, and hysteresis). Structural properties of a specific specimen — such as stiffness k = EA/L — depend on both material properties and geometry, which is why stress-strain normalization is essential for comparing tissues across specimens.


Bone and cartilage
Bone exists as dense compact (cortical) bone forming the outer shell, and porous trabecular (cancellous) bone forming the inner lattice at the ends of long bones; at the microscale, cortical bone is organized into osteons — concentric rings of mineral-reinforced collagen surrounding central vascular canals — that give bone its anisotropic mechanical properties. There are three types of cartilage: articular (hyaline) cartilage, which lines joint surfaces and achieves very low friction through fluid pressurization and glycoprotein boundary lubricants; elastic cartilage, found in structures such as the external ear; and fibrocartilage, found in the menisci and labra. The mechanical behavior of articular cartilage arises from its extracellular matrix: proteoglycans attract and retain interstitial fluid through Donnan osmotic pressure, and this fluid pressurization together with the tensile collagen network produces the tissue’s viscoelastic response. Limited vascularity and low cell density in fibrocartilaginous structures such as the meniscus explain why injuries to these tissues heal slowly.


Tendon, ligament, and muscle mechanics
Tendons connect muscle to bone with nearly parallel type I collagen fibers optimized for uniaxial tensile load transmission; ligaments connect bone to bone with a similar but slightly more varied fiber architecture that reflects their multidirectional loading demands. The low-stiffness toe region of both tissues’ stress-strain curves arises from the progressive recruitment and straightening of initially crimped collagen fibers; as strain increases, more fibers engage and stiffness rises until the tissue enters its linear elastic region. Muscle has passive mechanical properties arising primarily from the giant elastic protein titin and the extracellular matrix, and active force generated by sarcomeric actin-myosin cross-bridges; the active force-length relationship, force-velocity relationship, and passive force-length curve are the core empirical descriptors of muscle mechanics. Aging increases intramuscular collagen crosslinking and fat infiltration, reducing contractile fraction; muscle hypertrophy occurs through increased fiber cross-sectional area rather than through a meaningful increase in fiber number.


Experimental characterization and computational modeling
Material properties of musculoskeletal tissues cannot generally be derived analytically because they arise from complex microstructure; they are instead characterized empirically by applying controlled deformation to specimens while measuring force, then converting these to stress and strain. Testing configurations range from ex vivo cadaveric specimens to in situ setups that better preserve physiological boundary conditions; specimens can be loaded in multiple directions and at different rates to capture anisotropy and viscoelasticity. Where direct mechanical testing is impractical, computational finite element methods allow internal stresses and strains to be estimated under complex loading conditions. FEBio is an open-source finite element solver designed for biological materials, supporting hyperelastic, viscoelastic, biphasic, and multiphasic constitutive formulations suited to musculoskeletal tissues (Maas et al., 2012, PMID 22482660).

title: EMG filtering
text:
Overview

Introduction to Filter Theory
Digital filters exploit the fact that any signal can be represented as a sum of sine waves at different frequencies and amplitudes, selectively attenuating components in certain frequency bands while preserving others. The preserved frequency range is the pass band; the attenuated range is the stop band. Before selecting filter settings, examining the raw signal’s frequency composition via a Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) — comparing a baseline segment to an active segment — reveals where real signal energy lies and where noise peaks occur, and should inform filter design rather than simply copying settings from the literature.


Filter Types: High Pass, Low Pass, and Band Pass
A high-pass filter attenuates low-frequency components while preserving high-frequency ones, making it appropriate for removing DC offset and motion artifact from raw EMG. A low-pass filter does the reverse and is used to smooth a rectified EMG signal into an activation envelope. A band-pass filter combines both cutoffs — preserving a defined frequency window and discarding energy above and below it — and is appropriate when noise exists at both the low and high ends of the spectrum.


Common Sources of EMG Noise and the Physiological Signal Range
Motor unit action potentials span roughly 20–450 Hz, and this range guides EMG filter design. The principal noise sources are motion artifact (typically below 20–25 Hz; De Luca, Gilmore & Kuznetsov, 2010), AC electrical line noise (60 Hz in North America, 50 Hz elsewhere), cardiac artifact in recordings from muscles near the chest, and — in combined recordings — interference from adjacent instruments such as sonomicrometry systems at frequencies that depend on the system’s pulse repetition rate. Because the lower boundary of the physiological signal range overlaps with some noise sources, filter settings should be chosen from inspection of the data rather than copied from the literature without verification.


Filter Parameters: Cutoff Frequency and Filter Order
The cutoff frequency marks the transition between pass band and stop band; in MATLAB, it is specified normalized to the Nyquist frequency (sampling frequency ÷ 2). Filter order controls roll-off sharpness: higher orders produce steeper transitions but risk introducing ringing artifacts — transient oscillations that can push a filtered signal below zero in regions that are clearly positive in the raw data. MATLAB’s filtfilt function applies the filter forward and then backward for zero-phase filtering, which prevents time shifts in the filtered signal but doubles the effective filter order relative to the design specification.


Practical EMG Filtering in MATLAB
MATLAB’s Butterworth filter workflow uses buttord to determine the minimum order and cutoff frequency meeting specified performance criteria, butter to compute filter coefficients, and filtfilt for zero-phase application. For a high-pass filter, single stop-band and pass-band frequencies are provided; for a band-pass filter, vectors of two frequencies are provided for each parameter, and providing two values automatically configures MATLAB’s Butterworth functions for bandpass mode. After applying any filter, the raw and filtered signals should always be plotted together to verify that peak shape is preserved and that no ringing artifacts have been introduced; hardware filtering already applied by the data acquisition system can reduce the need for aggressive software filter settings.


Creating a Smooth Linear Envelope
After high-pass or band-pass filtering, the EMG signal is rectified (absolute value of each sample) to convert it to a fully positive representation. A second, low-pass filter applied to the rectified signal produces the smooth linear envelope most commonly shown in published figures; a widely used implementation is a 4th-order Butterworth at 10 Hz (Winter, 2009), achieved with a 2nd-order specification when using filtfilt. The high-pass or band-pass filter must always be applied to the raw, un-rectified signal first — applying it after rectification can introduce spurious negative deflections not present in the original data.


Surface EMG Considerations and Electrode Configuration
Surface EMG is typically sampled at approximately 1,000 Hz in line with SENIAM guidelines (Hermens et al., 2000), whereas indwelling electrodes often use higher sampling rates to capture a broader frequency range. Surface recordings are susceptible to crosstalk from adjacent muscles, and signal characteristics vary with electrode placement relative to the motor end plate; for precise frequency characterization at the individual muscle level, indwelling electrodes provide cleaner isolation. High-density electrode arrays — multiple electrodes in a grid configuration — offer a middle ground by enabling spatial decomposition of EMG components, analogous to spatial filtering in EEG.

title: Scaling and dimensional analysis
text:
Overview

Gait types and their mechanical signatures
Legged animals use only a small number of stereotyped movement patterns called gaits. For striding bipeds — including humans, ostriches, and most ground birds — the two primary gaits are walking and running. These gaits can be distinguished both by foot-contact timing and by the dynamics of the body’s center of mass.
Duty factor is the ratio of stance duration to stride duration and provides a concise gait descriptor. When duty factor exceeds 0.5, there is a period of double support in which both limbs contact the ground simultaneously; this is the hallmark of walking. When duty factor falls below 0.5, there is an aerial phase in which no limbs contact the ground; this characterizes running gaits. Some birds also use a grounded running gait, in which running-like spring dynamics occur at low duty factors that still retain brief periods of overlapping limb support — a gait not commonly observed in humans.
Walking — inverted pendulum dynamics. During walking, the body can be approximated as a point mass vaulting over a relatively stiff leg. As the leg contacts the ground, the body is moving fastest and at its lowest height; as it arcs over the stance leg to mid-stance, it rises to its greatest height and decelerates. Gravitational potential energy and kinetic energy therefore fluctuate out of phase, and this passive exchange reduces the external mechanical work required to move the center of mass. This inverted-pendulum mechanism makes the stance phase of walking mechanically economical.
Running — spring-mass dynamics. At higher speeds, the pattern reverses. The leg compresses like a spring during stance, so the body is at its lowest height at mid-stance rather than its highest. Kinetic energy and gravitational potential energy now fluctuate in phase — both decrease during the first half of stance and increase during the second half — making direct exchange between them impossible. Instead, energy is stored in and returned from elastic structures in the limb (tendons, ligaments, and musculotendinous units), analogous to a bouncing mass on a spring.


Physical models for walking and running
The mass-spring (or spring-mass) model represents the runner as a point mass supported by a single massless spring leg. Despite its simplicity, this model captures the ground-reaction-force magnitude and timing observed across a wide range of running animals and speeds.
A key limitation of the single-leg inverted-pendulum model of walking is that it predicts a smooth, single-humped vertical ground-reaction-force trace, whereas the measured force during human (and animal) walking has a characteristic double-humped, M-shaped profile. Geyer, Seyfarth, and Blickhan (2006) resolved this by extending the spring-mass model to two legs. Their two-legged spring model reproduces the M-shaped ground-reaction-force profile and demonstrates that walking gaits can be viewed as a spring-loaded inverted pendulum (SLIP), with the same basic leg-spring mechanics underlying both walking and running. The SLIP model has since become the standard template model for studying gait dynamics across species.


Geometric similarity and the scaling challenge
A foundational concept for comparing animals of different sizes is isometric scaling (also called geometric similarity): what happens to lengths, areas, and volumes when an animal is simply scaled up in size without changing shape?
If linear dimensions (such as leg length, L) scale up by some factor, then:

Cross-sectional area scales as L²
Volume (and, assuming constant tissue density, body mass) scales as L³

This creates a fundamental mechanical challenge with increasing body size. Muscular and skeletal strength is proportional to the cross-sectional area of tissues, which scales as L². Body weight, which must be supported and accelerated, scales as L³. The ratio of strength to body weight therefore scales as 1/L: larger animals are relatively weaker under isometric scaling. To compensate, larger animals tend to adopt a more upright, straighter-legged posture, which orients the skeleton more vertically and reduces the muscular force required to support body weight in stance.


The dynamic similarity hypothesis
Geometric similarity describes shape; it does not predict whether animals of different sizes move in functionally similar ways. To address locomotor function across size, Alexander and Jayes (1983) developed the dynamic similarity hypothesis: animals of different sizes move in dynamically similar ways — using mechanically equivalent gaits — if their dimensionless gait parameters are equivalent when normalized by an appropriate set of characteristic physical quantities.
This is both a theoretical prediction and an empirical hypothesis that can be tested with data. If locomotor function scales in a dynamically similar manner, size-related differences in absolute gait measures (stride frequency, stride length, speed) should disappear once the data are expressed as dimensionless quantities. Deviations from collapse reveal genuine functional differences across size.


Dimensionless quantities for locomotion analysis
The appropriate set of normalizing quantities for legged terrestrial locomotion can be derived from the physics of the spring-loaded inverted pendulum. The key physical parameters governing these dynamics are body mass (M), leg length (L), and gravitational acceleration (g). Using these as base quantities, dimensionless forms of all gait variables can be derived:



Quantity
Dimensionless form




Length / distance
Divide by L


Force
Divide by Mg


Time
Divide by \(\sqrt{L/g}\) (pendular period)


Frequency
Multiply by \(\sqrt{L/g}\)


Speed
Divide by \(\sqrt{gL}\)


Energy / work
Divide by MgL



McMahon and Cheng (1990) applied this normalizing framework to the spring-mass running model, formalizing dimensionless parameters for running mechanics that include dimensionless leg stiffness and dimensionless peak force in addition to dimensionless speed.
Froude number. A particularly important dimensionless quantity is the Froude number, defined as:
\[Fr = \frac{V^2}{gL}\]
The Froude number is the ratio of inertial (kinetic) energy to gravitational (potential) energy in the system, and its square root equals the dimensionless speed. The Froude number has a physical significance for walking: as a legged system using inverted-pendulum mechanics increases speed, the centripetal acceleration required to maintain contact with the ground during the arc of stance increases. When Fr = 1, this centripetal acceleration equals gravitational acceleration, and the system is on the verge of becoming airborne at mid-stance. Walking with purely inverted-pendulum dynamics is therefore physically impossible above Fr = 1; an aerial phase naturally emerges. Measured walk-to-run transitions in many animals occur near this theoretical limit, supporting the utility of the Froude number as a dimensionless speed benchmark.
Note that the dimensionless speed (V / \(\sqrt{gL}\)) equals the square root of the Froude number, so these two quantities are related but differ at values away from 1; some sources use one, some the other.


Scaling patterns in avian bipedal locomotion
Ground birds offer an excellent comparative system for testing dynamic similarity in locomotion. A compiled dataset spanning a 2,500-fold range in body mass — from painted quail to ostriches, drawing on 21 species from the literature — provides a rigorous test of whether dimensionless normalization collapses cross-species variation in gait (Daley & Birn-Jeffery 2018).
In absolute (SI) units, large birds operate at much lower stride frequencies and take longer strides than small birds, and maximum absolute speed increases with body size. These differences are expected simply from size.
After normalization to dimensionless quantities, two key patterns emerge:

The large variation in stride frequency across species compresses substantially, but the rank order inverts: large birds (ostriches) use relatively higher dimensionless stride frequencies than small birds (quail), the opposite of the absolute pattern.
Large birds use relatively shorter dimensionless stride lengths than small birds.

These patterns are consistent with differences in center-of-mass trajectory between size classes. Large birds tend to use a more vertically bouncy running gait, with greater vertical oscillation of the center of mass. Small birds tend to use a flatter center-of-mass trajectory with longer relative strides. The vertically bouncy gait of large birds is associated with reduced fore-aft ground-reaction-force fluctuations, which reduces the mechanical work demand per stride — a potential functional advantage at large body size.
Ostriches are notable outliers even within the large-bird category: they use exceptionally high relative stride frequencies, which has been interpreted as reflecting well-developed elastic energy storage and return mechanisms in the distal limb (tendons and ligaments) that may also assist in accelerating the leg during swing via elastic catapult mechanisms.


Practical considerations for cross-species and cross-population comparisons
Several analytical choices affect the validity of dimensionless normalization and should be made deliberately based on the task at hand.
Defining leg length. Standing hip height is the most commonly used measure of leg length in comparative locomotion studies, because it approximates the resting leg length and is straightforward to measure consistently across species. However, hip height conflates body size with posture: larger animals adopt more upright postures, so hip height grows faster than skeletal segment length with increasing body mass. Alternative approaches include using the sum of limb-segment lengths (which reflects maximum extension capacity and may be more appropriate for jumping analyses) or limb-segment lengths back-calculated assuming isometric scaling. The appropriate choice depends on which aspect of the mechanical task is most relevant.
Including or excluding the foot. Whether the foot should be included in leg length depends on how the animal contacts the ground during the task of interest. Plantigrade animals (full foot contact) have an effective leg length from hip to ankle during walking, but digitigrade or unguligrade animals contact the ground on their toes or hooves, functionally incorporating the foot or metatarsus into the leg. For activities like running where contact point and posture vary, measuring the hip-to-center-of-pressure distance during the actual task provides the most functionally relevant leg length.
Applying to individuals with atypical anatomy. The same first-principles reasoning applies when scaling analyses are extended to individuals whose anatomy differs from population norms — for example, in the context of para-athletes or individuals with limb differences. The key quantity to identify is the effective leg length for the specific task: the distance from the body’s center of mass to the point of ground contact, whatever the anatomy in between. Identifying this effective length, and understanding the physics of the task it governs, provides the foundation for meaningful comparison.
Measuring comparable speed ranges. Comparing maximum speed across species is methodologically difficult: the speed range an animal will use in a laboratory differs from what it achieves in overground conditions, and the conditions required to elicit true maximum effort differ by species. These sampling differences should be considered carefully when interpreting cross-species comparisons, particularly at the extremes of the speed distribution.

title: Cross-bridge kinetics & experimental system analysis methods
text:
Overview

Experimental preparations
Demembranated (chemically skinned) muscle fiber preparations are produced by removing the cell membrane, allowing the intracellular environment to be controlled entirely by the bathing solution—calcium concentration, ATP level, and ionic strength can be set independently. For cardiac studies, multicellular myocardial strips (roughly 100–500 µm wide and 400–1200 µm long) are dissected from ventricular tissue; for single skeletal fiber experiments, fibers are trimmed to approximately 2–3 mm in length with diameters in the range of 50–120 µm. Each preparation is mounted between a force transducer and a length-controlling motor, and sarcomere length is set directly by imaging the regular thick-and-thin-filament striations under light microscopy.


The cross-bridge cycle
Calcium binding to troponin C initiates thin filament activation by shifting tropomyosin from the blocked to the open state, exposing myosin-binding sites on actin (McKillop & Geeves, 1993). Myosin attaches to actin in a post-hydrolysis M·ADP·Pi state; Pi release is functionally coupled to the force-generating power stroke, though whether lever-arm rotation precedes or follows Pi exit remains under investigation (Lymn & Taylor, 1971; Dantzig et al., 1992; Woody et al., 2019). ADP release from the AM·ADP complex is the rate-limiting step for cross-bridge detachment and is strain-dependent—mechanical load slows ADP exit and prolongs the strongly-bound state, providing a mechanism by which force modulates cycling rate (Siemankowski et al., 1985; Nyitrai & Geeves, 2004). ATP binding to the rigor complex then causes rapid myosin detachment, followed by ATP hydrolysis to restore the high-actin-affinity pre-stroke state, completing the cycle.


Passive mechanics and the force-length relationship
Striated muscle generates both active (calcium-activated) force and passive (resting) force; the primary intracellular source of passive tension is titin, which dominates at moderate sarcomere lengths, while collagen in the perimysium and endomysium becomes the major contributor at longer lengths (Granzier & Irving, 1995; Wang et al., 1991). The active force-length relationship follows the classic Gordon-Huxley-Julian description: force rises along an ascending limb as thick-thin filament overlap increases, reaches a plateau at optimal overlap, then declines along a descending limb as overlap is lost at very long sarcomere lengths (Gordon et al., 1966). Total force at any sarcomere length is the sum of these active and passive contributions.


Length-dependent activation and the Frank-Starling mechanism
At the organ level, the Frank-Starling law describes how greater ventricular filling increases stroke volume; the cellular basis is length-dependent activation, in which increasing sarcomere length within the physiological range enhances both peak active force and calcium sensitivity—a leftward shift of the force-pCa curve—independent of changes in filament overlap (Kentish et al., 1986; Allen & Kentish, 1985). Cross-bridge kinetics contribute to this length dependence: at longer sarcomere lengths and higher internal forces, ADP release from the AM·ADP complex slows, prolonging cross-bridge attachment and increasing force per cross-bridge, likely because mechanical strain on the cross-bridge alters the geometry of the catalytic pocket. Conversely, shorter sarcomere lengths are associated with faster cross-bridge detachment, which may facilitate relaxation. Together, these sarcomere length-dependent changes in ADP release rate represent a kinetic contribution to the Frank-Starling mechanism that operates alongside calcium sensitivity and filament overlap effects.


Myosin isoforms and cross-bridge kinetic sensitivity
The predominant cardiac myosin isoform varies with body size: alpha-myosin heavy chain (alpha-MHC, MYH6), with its high ATPase rate and fast shortening velocity, dominates in small animals such as mice and rats, while beta-myosin heavy chain (beta-MHC, MYH7)—a slower, higher-economy isoform—predominates in larger animals including humans (Lompre et al., 1979). The magnitude of length-dependent kinetic sensitivity differs markedly with isoform: in skeletal muscle, slow-twitch (type I / beta-MHC) fibers show greater length-dependent calcium sensitivity than fast-twitch fibers, while fast-twitch myosin kinetics are comparatively insensitive to changes in sarcomere length. This isoform-dependent variation in length sensitivity may partly explain why the cellular expression of the Frank-Starling mechanism differs across species.


System analysis: sinusoidal perturbation, step-stretch, and the ABC model
In sinusoidal length perturbation analysis, the muscle is oscillated through a range of frequencies while force is recorded; the in-phase and out-of-phase components of the force response yield the elastic and viscous moduli, respectively, mapping kinetic processes that operate at different time scales (Kawai & Brandt, 1980). Step-stretch protocols apply a rapid length step and record the resulting multi-phase force transient—comprising a rapid elastic force rise (Phase 1), fast tension decay as stretched cross-bridges detach (Phase 2), and slower tension recovery as new cross-bridges recruit (Phase 3)—providing estimates of cross-bridge attachment and detachment kinetics from a shorter activation period (Huxley & Simmons, 1971; Ford, Huxley, & Simmons, 1977). Frequency-domain sinusoidal data are typically fit to the three-component ABC model of Kawai and Brandt (1980), in which Process A reflects slow regulatory dynamics, Process B reflects cross-bridge recruitment, and Process C reflects the force-generating kinetic step, providing estimates of Pi-release rates and cross-bridge attachment time. MATLAB scripts developed in the Tanner lab implement fitting routines for both sinusoidal and step-stretch data, extracting ABC process parameters and estimating ADP release and ATP binding rates across fiber types and species.

title: Getting Started in Movement Science
text:
For: Newcomers to movement science  |  5 modules  |  ~7.5 hours
Movement science draws on anatomy, mechanics, computation, and statistics to understand how animals — including humans — produce and control movement. This pathway is designed for learners who are new to the field and want to build a solid foundation across all four of those threads. The five workshops are sequenced to introduce the biology of muscle first, then the mechanical principles that govern the musculoskeletal system, then the research and computational tools you will need to study it rigorously. No prior background in biomechanics or programming is assumed.
Click through the tabs below to preview the learning objectives and content of each module, then follow the link to the full workshop.

1. Muscle Anatomy & Physiology2. Musculoskeletal Mechanics3. Best Practices in Scientific Programming4. Data Visualization & Statistical Inference5. Simulating Movement


Presented by: Dr. Jenna Monroy

Learning objectives
By the end of this workshop, you should be able to:

Describe the hierarchical organization of skeletal muscle from the whole organ to the sarcomere level, including the roles of key structural proteins — actin, myosin, and titin — in generating and regulating force.
Explain the fundamental muscle properties (excitation-contraction coupling, force-length, force-velocity, and force-frequency relationships), identify how each is measured, and articulate the limitations of applying static measurements to predict dynamic movement.
Evaluate how variation in muscle architecture, fiber type, sarcomere structure, and titin isoform expression tunes muscle function across muscles and across species.



Overview
The muscular system is one of the most highly conserved systems across the animal kingdom, with fundamental mechanisms of force generation that are remarkably similar from insects to large mammals. At the same time, a single muscle can function as a motor, spring, brake, or strut depending on how it is controlled — and subtle differences in protein isoforms, architecture, or neural control can substantially alter whole-animal performance. This workshop builds the biological vocabulary and conceptual framework that all subsequent movement science topics depend on.
Go to full workshop →



Presented by: Dr. Katie Knaus

Learning objectives
By the end of this workshop, you should be able to:

Define stress, strain, and Young’s modulus, and explain how these quantities characterize the mechanical behavior of musculoskeletal tissues.
Identify the main connective tissue types in the musculoskeletal system — bone, cartilage, tendon, and ligament — and describe how their microstructure determines their mechanical properties.
Classify joint degrees of freedom and describe how internal loads (tension, compression, bending, torsion) are distributed within biological structures.



Overview
Mechanics is the study of how bodies react to forces. The musculoskeletal system is subject to forces from gravity, ground contact, and muscle contractions, which combine to produce internal loads in bones, tendons, and ligaments. Understanding these principles helps explain why tissues fail, how joints are designed, and what trade-offs are built into biological structures — providing the physical reasoning behind phenomena that might otherwise seem arbitrary.
Go to full workshop →



Presented by: Dr. James Finley

Learning objectives
By the end of this workshop, you should be able to:

Design a consistent file and folder structure for a scientific study, including naming conventions that support automated analysis and long-term reuse of data.
Structure a data analysis pipeline as a series of separate, clearly named scripts — each performing a distinct step — moving from raw data through summary statistics and figure creation.
Write readable, reusable code using functions and meaningful variable names, and apply unit testing to verify that code produces correct results.



Overview
Good programming practices matter because scientific work can be elegant but fragile when built on weak foundations. Two recurring failure modes motivate this workshop: a researcher who cannot reproduce their own analysis months later, and data or code that becomes unusable after a student moves on. The practices covered here — protocol documentation, consistent file structures, modular pipelines, and readable code — address both problems before they arise.
Go to full workshop →



Presented by: Dr. James Finley

Learning objectives
By the end of this workshop, you should be able to:

Explain why descriptive statistics alone can be misleading and why visualizing data at every stage of analysis is essential for drawing valid conclusions.
Describe what a p-value represents, how the false positive rate relates to the conventional significance threshold of p < 0.05, and why statistical significance does not imply practical importance.
Identify how sample size, statistical power, and effect size are related, and recognize that small studies are best positioned to detect large effects.



Overview
Statistics serve as tools for quantifying and explaining variability — but they can mislead when used without careful thought. Anscombe’s Quartet famously illustrates how four visually distinct data sets can have nearly identical summary statistics, making the fitted model appear valid when it is not. This workshop builds the critical thinking needed to visualize first, analyze second, and interpret results with appropriate uncertainty.
Go to full workshop →



Presented by: Dr. Christian Hubicki

Learning objectives
By the end of this workshop, you should be able to:

Explain that simulating movement means numerically solving differential equations that describe how a system’s state changes over time.
Apply Euler’s method to step a simple first-order ordinary differential equation forward in time using a small, fixed time step.
Describe how to convert a second-order equation of motion into a system of first-order ODEs using state variables, and identify the state vector for a simple spring-mass system.



Overview
Computer simulations complement physical experiments by allowing researchers to test hypotheses and explore conditions that would be impossible or unethical to impose on a live animal. Simulation means numerically solving differential equations that describe how a system’s state changes over time — a skill that opens the door to computational movement science and connects directly to the biological and mechanical foundations introduced in the earlier workshops in this pathway.
Go to full workshop →

title: Muscle Mechanics & Modeling
text:
For: Learners with a basic foundation in muscle biology  |  6 modules  |  ~7.5 hours
This pathway goes beneath the surface of muscle function to examine how force is produced at the molecular level, how the mechanical properties of muscle and tendon are measured and characterized, and how computational models capture these phenomena across scales. The first four workshops move from the biochemistry of the cross-bridge cycle through the mechanics of the muscle-tendon unit and into the computational frameworks used to simulate and interrogate both. A fifth, more specialized module introduces synchrotron X-ray diffraction — a powerful structural imaging technique that underpins much of what is known about the sarcomere at the molecular level.
Click through the tabs below to preview the learning objectives and content of each module, then follow the link to the full workshop.

1. Cross-bridge Kinetics2. System Identification3. Series Elasticity4. Computational Modeling5. X-ray Diffraction ✦6. Work Loops 101


Presented by: Dr. Bert Tanner & Maddy Chastain

Learning objectives
By the end of this workshop, you should be able to:

Describe the major biochemical steps of the actomyosin cross-bridge cycle and explain how phosphate release, ADP release, and ATP binding govern force production and cross-bridge detachment.
Explain how sinusoidal length perturbation analysis and step-stretch protocols are used to estimate cross-bridge attachment and detachment rates in demembranated fiber preparations, and interpret the elastic and viscous modulus outputs in terms of the ABC process model.
Relate sarcomere length-dependent changes in cross-bridge kinetics to the cellular basis of the Frank-Starling mechanism and discuss how myosin isoform composition influences the magnitude of this length dependence.



Overview
Force production in striated muscle is driven by the cyclic interaction of myosin with actin. The sequence of molecular events — calcium activation of the thin filament, myosin binding, the power stroke, and detachment — can be probed directly using demembranated fiber preparations, in which the cell membrane is removed so that the intracellular environment is controlled entirely by the experimenter. Sinusoidal length perturbation analysis and step-stretch protocols applied to these preparations allow researchers to estimate the rates at which cross-bridges attach and detach, and to ask how those rates change with sarcomere length, myosin isoform, and applied load. This workshop covers both the mechanochemical model underlying force generation and the experimental methods used to test it.
Go to full workshop →



Presented by: Dr. Kiisa Nishikawa & Dr. Adwait Mane

Learning objectives
By the end of this workshop, you should be able to:

Describe the difference between first-principles modeling and system identification, and explain when each approach is appropriate for studying biological tissues.
Identify the components of simple viscoelastic models (spring, damper, Maxwell, Kelvin-Voigt) and predict how each element responds to a step stretch or a step force input.
Explain how ramp stretch experiments and transfer functions are used to estimate the viscoelastic properties of muscle and tendon, and describe how those properties relate to energy storage, power amplification, and tissue structure.



Overview
Muscle and tendon are viscoelastic materials: they resist both deformation (like a spring) and rate of deformation (like a damper), and their mechanical behavior depends on the history of loading. System identification is the process of building mathematical models of a dynamical system from experimentally measured input-output data — in this case, using controlled length inputs and recorded force outputs to identify the spring-damper network that best describes each tissue. This workshop introduces the transfer-function framework, the spring-damper building blocks, and the model-selection criteria used to compare candidate descriptions, and presents empirical findings from ramp-stretch experiments on a range of muscle and tendon preparations.
Go to full workshop →



Presented by: Dr. Manny Azizi

Learning objectives
By the end of this workshop, you should be able to:

Describe the hierarchical collagen structure of tendon and explain how the crimped resting arrangement of collagen fibers gives rise to the nonlinear (toe region) stress-strain behavior that characterizes viscoelastic connective tissue.
Distinguish among the three functional roles of in-series elastic elements during locomotion — power conservation, power amplification, and power attenuation — and identify the mechanical and biological conditions that favor each role.
Explain how the mechanical matching of muscle force capacity and tendon stiffness influences energy storage during explosive movements, and how body size constrains the benefit of spring-driven versus direct muscle actuation.



Overview
Tendons and aponeuroses are not passive conduits — they store and return mechanical energy, and in some movements they can release energy faster than the muscle alone could deliver it. These elastic structures appear across virtually the entire animal kingdom, from invertebrate spring-loaded mechanisms to the large free tendons of running vertebrates. Understanding their function requires thinking carefully about how stiffness, length, and force capacity are matched between muscle and tendon, and about how scaling with body size changes the trade-offs. This workshop develops the mechanical vocabulary for in-series elastic elements and uses it to interpret locomotor strategies across species.
Go to full workshop →



Presented by: Dr. Bert Tanner

Learning objectives
By the end of this workshop, you should be able to:

Understand how computational models of muscle contraction have evolved from whole-muscle mechanical descriptions (such as the Hill model) to spatially explicit, molecular-level simulations of actin-myosin cross-bridge interactions.
Explain how the mechanical properties of thick and thin filaments — specifically their elasticity and compliance — affect the probability of cross-bridge binding and the amount of force produced within a sarcomere.
Recognize how the physiological geometry of the sarcomere filament lattice (multiple interacting thick and thin filaments) amplifies cross-bridge recruitment and force output compared to simpler two-filament models.



Overview
No single experiment can observe all the moving parts of a contracting sarcomere simultaneously. Computational models fill that gap by representing the molecular interactions explicitly and allowing researchers to ask “what if” questions that are impossible or impractical to test in the lab. This workshop traces the history of muscle models from A.V. Hill’s phenomenological three-component model through Huxley’s cross-bridge theory to spatially explicit Monte Carlo simulations that account for filament compliance and the full hexagonal lattice geometry of the sarcomere. A MATLAB implementation of the two-filament model is available for hands-on exploration, making this a natural entry point for learners who want to build or modify muscle simulations of their own.
Go to full workshop →



Presented by: Dr. Jiangkun Wei, Casey King & Dr. Simon Sponberg

Specialized topic. This module covers a highly technical, facility-dependent technique used by a subset of muscle biology labs. It is not required to follow the rest of the pathway — but if you want to understand how researchers actually see cross-bridges move in real time, it is one of the most exciting tools in the field.


Learning objectives
By the end of this workshop, you should be able to:

Recognize the main features of a muscle X-ray diffraction pattern — equatorial reflections, meridional reflections, and layer lines — and connect each feature to the underlying structural periodicity in the sarcomere.
Apply Bragg’s law to convert the angular position of a diffraction reflection into a real-space structural spacing in the myofilament lattice.
Describe how synchrotron X-ray sources make it possible to record diffraction patterns from living, contracting muscle at millisecond timescales.



Overview
The cross-bridge cycle unfolds at nanometer scales and millisecond timescales — far below what light microscopy can resolve and inaccessible to electron microscopy without chemical fixation that kills the preparation. Synchrotron X-ray diffraction fills this gap: by exploiting the constructive interference of X-rays scattered from the regular hexagonal lattice of thick and thin filaments, it can measure lattice spacings and cross-bridge mass distribution in living, contracting muscle in real time. Equatorial reflections report on radial filament spacing and cross-bridge attachment state; meridional reflections and layer lines reveal axial periodicities of the myosin and actin helices. It was this structural evidence — changes in filament compliance and lattice geometry during contraction — that motivated the spatially explicit computational models in the previous module, making this workshop a rewarding complement for anyone who wants to understand where those models came from.

title: Neural Control & Balance
text:
For: Learners interested in neuromechanics and motor control  |  3 modules  |  ~4.5 hours
Controlling movement requires the nervous system to continuously sense the body’s state, integrate that information across multiple sensory channels, and issue corrective commands fast enough to prevent a fall. This pathway traces that process from the top down — starting with the big picture of how the brain combines sensory signals and organizes balance responses, then zooming into the proprioceptive receptor at the heart of that sensing, and finally examining how stability and agility are defined and measured as biomechanical quantities in the lab.
Click through the tabs below to preview the learning objectives and content of each module, then follow the link to the full workshop.

1. The Brain and Balance2. Modeling the Muscle Spindle3. Balance, Stability & Agility


Presented by: Dr. Lena Ting

Learning objectives
By the end of this workshop, you should be able to:

Identify the four major sensory systems that contribute to balance — vision, vestibular, cutaneous, and proprioception — and explain why no single system provides sufficient information on its own.
Describe how the brain’s hierarchical control of balance (spinal cord, brainstem, cortex) shifts from automatic to voluntary processing as task difficulty increases or as aging and neurological disease progress.
Explain why cognitive flexibility and motor adaptability are linked, and how both relate to fall risk in older adults and people with neurological conditions such as Parkinson’s disease.



Overview
Balance is normally automatic — governed by subcortical circuits without conscious effort. But maintaining it requires the nervous system to integrate signals from vision, the vestibular system, cutaneous receptors in the feet, and proprioceptors in the muscles, because no single channel can fully answer whether the body is falling or what its configuration is. These signals are processed through a hierarchy of circuits: the spinal cord generates fast joint-level reflexes, the brainstem integrates whole-body falling direction and selects the appropriate muscle strategy across multiple joints, and the cortex handles deliberate adaptation when automatic responses are insufficient. As aging or disease erodes the efficiency of lower circuits, balance demands more cortical attention — narrowing the cognitive resources available for other tasks and elevating fall risk.
Go to full workshop →



Presented by: Dr. Surabhi Simha

Learning objectives
By the end of this workshop, you should be able to:

Identify the anatomical components of the muscle spindle — intrafusal fiber types, afferent types, and fusimotor inputs — and explain the role each plays in generating sensory signals.
Describe why muscle spindle Ia afferent firing is history-dependent and how cross-bridge dynamics provide a mechanistic explanation for this behavior.
Trace the flow of inputs and outputs through the biophysical spindle model, from muscle tendon unit length and motor activations to receptor potential, and distinguish between forward simulation and optimization modes.



Overview
Proprioception — the sense of body position and movement — depends on specialized sensory structures called muscle spindles embedded within skeletal muscle. Each spindle contains intrafusal muscle fibers innervated by both sensory (afferent) and motor (fusimotor) axons, allowing the nervous system not only to read muscle length and velocity but to adjust the sensitivity of the receptor itself. A key feature of spindle firing is that it is history-dependent: the same length can produce different firing rates depending on prior movement, a phenomenon that cross-bridge dynamics in the intrafusal fibers help explain. This workshop covers spindle anatomy, the mechanistic basis of Ia afferent signals, and a biophysical model that can be run in both forward-simulation and optimization modes.
Go to full workshop →



Presented by: Dr. Greg Sawicki

Learning objectives
By the end of this workshop, you will be able to:

Describe at least four methods researchers use to measure balance during walking — including step placement predictability, angular momentum regulation, margin of stability, and center-of-mass displacement — and explain why perturbation experiments are important for studying balance effectively.
Explain how ankle exoskeleton assistance can be timed to improve standing balance recovery, and describe the role of whole-body center-of-mass-level control in balance, as distinct from purely local ankle reflexes.
Distinguish between stability (how quickly a system returns to a steady movement pattern after an unexpected perturbation) and agility (how quickly a system transitions to a new movement target on purpose), and understand how both can be defined and measured using energy-based metrics.



Overview
Studying balance in the lab requires choosing metrics carefully — not all of them are equally sensitive to impairment. A systematic comparison of six common measures found that step placement predictability outperformed the others, while center-of-mass displacement alone performed no better than chance at detecting imbalance. Beyond which metric to use, this workshop develops a principled framework for what stability and agility actually mean: stability is the rate at which a system’s energy returns to a nominal limit cycle after a perturbation, and agility is the rate at which it transitions to a new target. Defining both in a common energy currency makes it possible to compare the costs of stabilization, intentional transitions, and metabolic efficiency within one framework — and to ask how assistive devices such as exoskeletons can best be timed to support balance recovery.
Go to full workshop →

title: Experimental Methods
text:
For: Learners preparing to collect or analyze movement data  |  5 modules  |  ~6 hours
Movement science research depends on a toolkit of measurement techniques, each suited to different questions, settings, and scales of analysis. This pathway surveys four of the most widely used approaches — from clinical and video-based assessment tools accessible outside the lab, to marker-based motion capture and EMG, to structural imaging of muscle during movement. The modules share a common theme but do not follow a strict sequence; start with the technique most relevant to your work.
Click through the tabs below to preview the learning objectives and content of each module, then follow the link to the full workshop.

Movement ExplorationMotion Capture & EMGEMG FilteringUltrasound ImagingWork Loops 101


Presented by: Dr. Jill McNitt-Gray & Dr. Kelli Sharp

Learning objectives
By the end of this workshop, you should be able to:

Identify validated tools for assessing functional mobility and markerless motion capture, including their appropriate clinical and research applications.
Explain how psychophysiological and virtual reality methods are used to study anxiety-related movement behaviors, including kinesiophobia.
Recognize the measurement limitations of standard balance scales, including ceiling and floor effects, when selecting outcome measures across diverse populations.



Overview
Not all movement research happens in a motion capture lab. This workshop surveys assessment approaches that extend into clinical and naturalistic settings. The Timed Up and Go (TUG) test is one of the most widely used clinical tools for measuring functional mobility, though like many standardized scales it can exhibit ceiling and floor effects that limit its sensitivity across populations with widely varying ability. Markerless pose estimation tools — including AlphaPose and DeepLabCut — allow researchers to extract joint kinematics directly from ordinary video, removing the need for physical markers and lowering the barrier for data collection in the field. The workshop also covers psychophysiological methods for studying how anxiety shapes movement: electrodermal activity as an index of sympathetic arousal, the clinical construct of kinesiophobia, and virtual reality as a safe and controllable way to induce height-related anxiety in balance and gait research.
Go to full workshop →



Presented by: Lauren Infantino, Kennedy Kerr, Autumn Routt & Emily Smith

Learning objectives
By the end of this workshop, you should be able to:

Explain how inverse kinematics and inverse dynamics are used to compute joint angles and joint moments from motion capture data, and identify the assumptions underlying each approach.
Describe how muscle action potentials are detected by bipolar electrodes and how surface EMG signals reflect the summed activity of multiple motor units.
Identify common sources of error in motion capture and EMG data collection and describe practical strategies to minimize them at each stage of the processing pipeline.



Overview
Motion capture and surface EMG are the paired workhorses of movement science labs: one tracks the kinematics of the skeleton, the other records the electrical activity of the muscles driving it. Neither measurement is direct — joint angles are computed from marker trajectories via inverse kinematics, joint moments via inverse dynamics, and EMG signals reflect a summed electrical field from many motor units rather than a single muscle’s output. Error introduced at any step in the pipeline accumulates through every subsequent computation, making careful data collection and protocol design essential. This workshop covers the underlying math and physiology of both techniques, common failure modes (soft tissue artifact, electrode cross-talk, marker occlusion), and the practical recommendations that minimize their impact.
Go to full workshop →



Presented by: Dr. Monica Daley

Learning objectives
By the end of this workshop, you should be able to:

Distinguish between high pass, low pass, and band pass filters, and identify when each type is appropriate for EMG data.
Describe the two key filter parameters — cutoff frequency and filter order — and explain the trade-off between filter sharpness and artifact risk.
Outline the standard EMG processing pipeline: apply a high pass or band pass filter to raw data, rectify, and optionally create a smooth linear envelope.



Overview
A raw EMG signal contains the muscle activity you want along with motion artifact, DC offset, and high-frequency noise you do not. Filtering is the step that separates them — but choosing the wrong settings can remove real signal, create ringing artifacts, or blur the timing of muscle bursts. This workshop builds the conceptual foundation for filter design in the frequency domain: what a Bode plot reveals, how cutoff frequency and filter order interact, and how to use a Fast Fourier Transform to inspect your data before choosing settings rather than copying defaults from the literature. The standard processing pipeline — bandpass filter, rectify, low-pass envelope — is covered step by step, with attention to the decisions that most commonly introduce errors in practice.
Go to full workshop →



Presented by: Dr. Luke Jessup

Learning objectives
By the end of this workshop, you should be able to:

Describe how ultrasound imaging works and explain how different tissue types — including muscle, tendon, bone, nerve, and blood vessels — can be distinguished from one another in an ultrasound image.
Explain why tracking muscle fascicle length and velocity matters for understanding a muscle’s force-generating capacity and its role in whole-body movement efficiency.
Identify the key steps involved in using fascicle tracking software to extract length measurements from ultrasound video data, and describe the trade-offs between optical flow and line detection approaches.



Overview
Ultrasound imaging makes it possible to observe muscle fascicles moving in real time during walking, running, and jumping — measurements that would otherwise require invasive procedures. Because force production depends on fascicle length and shortening velocity relative to the muscle’s optimum, knowing where a muscle operates on its force-length and force-velocity curves during natural movement is key to understanding why people move the way they do. This workshop covers how ultrasound works (echogenicity, B-mode imaging, tissue identification), the practicalities of strapping flat-form probes to a moving limb, synchronization with motion capture and force data, and the two main automated fascicle tracking approaches implemented in MATLAB — optical flow and line detection — along with guidance on when each is appropriate.
